purpose: Ground Ask AI answers in the volumes actually present on the C.O.M.I.C.S. shelves.
rules: Recommend shelf volumes by exact shelf id only.
Reception fields report reader and critical consensus, not objective fact.
Full guided tours are available on demand through read_tour(hero_id).
C.O.M.I.C.S. contains cover images, not interior comic pages.

tone_modes.label: Strangest, and most anxious
tone_modes.description: Ditko's New York — a nervous kid, uncanny villains, and a hero who crouches. The furthest from the modern character and the most distinctive book on the shelf.

tone_modes.label: Most romantic
tone_modes.description: Romita Sr.'s soap opera. College, two women, a supporting cast with faces. This is the Spider-Man most people carry in their head.

tone_modes.label: Bleakest
tone_modes.description: The Conway years, and the bridge. The book learns that the hero can do everything right and lose anyway, and it never fully recovers.

tone_modes.label: Best made
tone_modes.description: Stern's run — short, and story for story the most consistently excellent stretch anyone has written. Start here if you want proof the character works.

tone_modes.label: Warmest
tone_modes.description: Busiek and Olliffe writing new 1964 comics in 1995. No angst, no continuity to know, and a real fondness for the material it is imitating.

tone_modes.label: Most 1990s
tone_modes.description: Art as the product. Impossible poses, webbing everywhere, Venom on every other cover, and a book that sold two million copies on a signature.

tone_modes.label: Most notorious
tone_modes.description: The Clone Saga. Read it as a document of what happens when a story is not allowed to end — and for Ben Reilly, who deserved better.

tone_modes.label: Most cinematic
tone_modes.description: Decompressed, conversational, built for the trade paperback. Two very different answers to how you make a sixty-year-old character legible again.

tone_modes.label: Saddest ending
tone_modes.description: The only book here that gets to finish, and the reason Miles Morales exists.

volumes.title: Amazing Spider-Man Omnibus
volumes.creators: Stan Lee & Steve Ditko
volumes.note: The complete Lee/Ditko run. Everything Spider-Man is starts here — Amazing Fantasy #15 through the Master Planner saga and Ditko's exit.
volumes.lede: The Lee and Ditko run, which is stranger, sadder and more idiosyncratic than its reputation — and much more Ditko's book than the credits box suggests.
volumes.verdict: One of the small handful of Silver Age runs that is genuinely still read for pleasure rather than for history, and the consensus is that it gets better as it goes — the first ten issues are finding their feet, and by the twenties the book is extraordinary.

volumes.title: Amazing Spider-Man Omnibus
volumes.creators: Stan Lee & John Romita Sr.
volumes.note: Romita takes over. The Green Goblin's identity, Mary Jane's entrance, the Kingpin's debut, and "Spider-Man No More!"
volumes.lede: Romita Sr. takes over and the best-selling superhero comic in America turns into a romance book with fights in it.
volumes.verdict: Beloved, and the site of the shelf's oldest argument: Ditko or Romita. Both camps are large and both are right about something — Romita's Spider-Man is warmer, better drawn as pure craft, and vastly more popular; Ditko's is stranger and more personal.

volumes.title: Amazing Spider-Man Omnibus
volumes.creators: Lee, Romita Sr. & Gil Kane
volumes.note: The Stone Tablet saga, Captain Stacy's death, the Comics Code-defying drug issues, and Morbius's debut.
volumes.lede: The end of the Lee era, Gil Kane's arrival, and the three issues that forced the Comics Code to rewrite itself.
volumes.verdict: Rated a notch below the two volumes either side of it as pure reading, and well ahead of them as history. The drug issues are the reason people buy it, and readers routinely report being slightly underwhelmed by them as stories — the significance is the publishing act, not the script.

volumes.title: Amazing Spider-Man Omnibus
volumes.creators: Gerry Conway & Ross Andru
volumes.note: The Night Gwen Stacy Died, the death of the Green Goblin, and the first Punisher and Clone Saga.
volumes.lede: Gwen Stacy dies, the Punisher arrives, and superhero comics stop being able to promise that the hero gets there in time.
volumes.verdict: #121–122 is on essentially every best-Spider-Man-story list ever assembled, and its status as a turning point for the whole medium is about as settled as these things get.

volumes.title: Untold Tales of Spider-Man Omnibus
volumes.creators: Kurt Busiek & Pat Olliffe
volumes.note: Published 1995–97 but set between the early Lee/Ditko issues. Slots here by story chronology, not print date — read it alongside Omnibus Vol. 1 or straight after.
volumes.lede: New comics written in 1995 and set inside 1963, at 99 cents, while the Clone Saga was happening in the room next door. The shelf's biggest sleeper.
volumes.verdict: Consistently described as underrated and better than it needed to be, and it is one of the books long-time Spider-Man readers recommend to people who bounced off the modern character.

volumes.title: Spider-Man by Roger Stern Omnibus
volumes.creators: Roger Stern, JRJR & John Byrne
volumes.note: The Hobgoblin mystery, "The Kid Who Collects Spider-Man," and Nothing Can Stop the Juggernaut.
volumes.lede: The shortest great run on the character, and story for story the best-made comics on this shelf.
volumes.verdict: Stern is very widely named the best Spider-Man writer after Lee, and this run is the reason. Reader polls routinely place three separate stories from it in the character's all-time top ten, which no other run manages.

volumes.title: ASM by Michelinie & McFarlane Omnibus
volumes.creators: David Michelinie & Todd McFarlane
volumes.note: ASM #300 — the first full Venom. McFarlane's run that reset what a Spider-Man comic looked like.
volumes.lede: Venom's debut, and the year a penciller became bigger than the character he was drawing.
volumes.verdict: One of the most commercially significant runs Marvel ever published, and the reception splits cleanly along a line that has not moved in thirty-five years: McFarlane's art is either the most exciting thing that ever happened to the book or the moment it went wrong.

volumes.title: Spider-Man by Michelinie & Larsen Omnibus
volumes.creators: David Michelinie & Erik Larsen
volumes.note: Picks up directly from the McFarlane omnibus. Overlaps it at ASM #324, #327 and #329.
volumes.lede: Same writer, same era, a completely different artist — which makes this the most useful comparison book on the shelf.
volumes.verdict: Warmly regarded and not much argued about. Larsen has a real following — largely from Savage Dragon, which he has drawn single-handed for over thirty years — and readers who find McFarlane's work airless tend to prefer this.

volumes.title: Spider-Man by Todd McFarlane Omnibus
volumes.creators: Todd McFarlane
volumes.note: The adjectiveless Spider-Man #1 — one of the best-selling comics ever printed — and McFarlane's solo writer/artist run.
volumes.lede: The best-selling comic book ever printed, and a document of the exact moment the industry decided the artist was the product.
volumes.verdict: Enormously important and not, on the whole, well loved. The standard assessment is that the art is extraordinary and the writing is thin — Torment in particular gets cited for mood over substance and for lettering tics that have not aged gracefully.

volumes.title: Spider-Man vs. Venom Omnibus
volumes.creators: David Michelinie & various
volumes.note: Every Venom appearance from the black suit's origin through Maximum Carnage, so it doubles back across the two Michelinie volumes above — ASM #300 and #315–317 are also in the McFarlane book, #332–333 and #346–347 in the Larsen one. Maximum Carnage is printed in crossover order, interleaving Amazing, Web, Spider-Man and Spectacular month by month.
volumes.lede: A decade of one relationship, assembled as a chronology rather than a run — the black costume's arrival through Maximum Carnage.
volumes.verdict: Judged mostly as a collection decision rather than a run, and on that basis it does well: the chronology is the right one, and having the black-suit material and the Venom escalation in a single volume is genuinely useful.

volumes.title: Spider-Man: Clone Saga Omnibus
volumes.creators: Various
volumes.note: Printed in true crossover reading order — Web, Amazing, Spider-Man and Spectacular interleave month by month, which is how the chapters below are grouped.
volumes.lede: The most notorious storyline in the character's history, from the top. It is worth reading, and it is worth knowing what you are reading.
volumes.verdict: The standard shorthand for a story that went wrong, and the criticisms are specific rather than vague: it ran far longer than it was ever plotted to, it required four books a month to follow, the mystery villains (Judas Traveller, Scrier) resolved to very little, and the central premise told readers that the character they had followed for thirty years was a fake.

volumes.title: Spider-Man: Clone Saga Omnibus
volumes.creators: Various
volumes.note: Maximum Clonage and the Jackal's endgame. Also interleaved in reading order.
volumes.lede: The middle, where the story stops being about identity and starts being about publishing.
volumes.verdict: Widely treated as the weakest stretch of an already contentious story, and the reasons given are consistent: too many clones, a proliferation of plot threads nobody was tracking, and the sense that the story was being extended rather than told.

volumes.title: Spider-Man: Ben Reilly Omnibus
volumes.creators: Various
volumes.note: Ben Reilly takes over as Spider-Man. The Scarlet Spider titles and the Sensational relaunch.
volumes.lede: The year Marvel actually did it: Peter Parker walked away and somebody else was Spider-Man in every book.
volumes.verdict: The most consistent revisionist position on the whole Clone Saga is that Ben Reilly was good and deserved better, and this volume is where the argument lives. Readers who disliked everything around it will still defend the character.

volumes.title: Amazing Spider-Man by J. Michael Straczynski Omnibus
volumes.creators: J. Michael Straczynski & John Romita Jr.
volumes.note: The post-9/11 relaunch. Ezekiel and the totem question, Aunt May finding out, and "The Conversation."
volumes.lede: A television writer takes the main book, asks whether the spider bite was ever the explanation, and gets four excellent years and one very bad decision.
volumes.verdict: The first half is very highly regarded — commonly named the best Amazing Spider-Man since Stern, with the Romita Jr. issues singled out and the Aunt May revelation treated as a landmark.

volumes.title: Ultimate Spider-Man Omnibus
volumes.creators: Brian Michael Bendis & Mark Bagley
volumes.note: A separate continuity, not the next chapter of the one above — the origin retold for 2000. Bendis and Bagley from #1 through the Venom arc and Gwen Stacy's death.
volumes.lede: Start him over at fifteen with no continuity, tell it slowly, and let one artist draw all of it. It worked better than anyone expected.
volumes.verdict: One of the most successful reinventions in superhero comics, and generally credited with proving that a legacy character could be restarted without being cheapened. Its DNA is visible in most Spider-Man screen adaptations since.

volumes.title: Death of Ultimate Spider-Man Omnibus
volumes.creators: Brian Michael Bendis & Mark Bagley
volumes.note: The end of Ultimate Peter Parker. Jumps well past the volume above — the 100-odd issues between the two are not collected in omnibus.
volumes.lede: The only book on this shelf that gets a real ending, and the one that produced Miles Morales.
volumes.verdict: Treated as a rare superhero death that earned its ending, largely because it was allowed to stand and because a decade of consistent storytelling had built to it. The issues immediately following, dealing with the fallout, are often rated higher than the death itself.

tone_modes.label: Most Jekyll-and-Hyde
tone_modes.description: The transformation as a curse the character is fighting, with real dread attached. The 1962 issues invented it; Immortal Hulk is the version that takes it most seriously.

tone_modes.label: Most sad-giant, most Bronze Age
tone_modes.description: A lonely, hunted, fundamentally gentle creature wandering the world. Trimpe's seven years are the purest expression of it and the reason this is what most people picture.

tone_modes.label: Funniest
tone_modes.description: The Joe Fixit years — the grey Hulk as a Las Vegas leg-breaker in a good suit. A genuine crime comedy, and unlike anything else here.

tone_modes.label: Most psychological
tone_modes.description: Multiple personalities treated as a clinical problem rather than a plot device, plus the articulate merged Hulk who can hold a conversation and lead a team.

tone_modes.label: Most paranoid
tone_modes.description: Banner on the run, conspiracies, the monster mostly off-panel. A thriller that happens to have the Hulk in it.

tone_modes.label: Most cosmic
tone_modes.description: Sword-and-planet adventure, then an invasion. The only period where he is the protagonist with a plan rather than the problem.

tone_modes.label: Loudest
tone_modes.description: Blockbuster slugfests drawn for maximum poster value. No subtext, no apology.

tone_modes.label: Scariest
tone_modes.description: Body horror, night, and a creature that comes back. The modern classic, and the one that most changes how the older books read.

tone_modes.label: Bleakest
tone_modes.description: The Maestro — the Hulk who won, ruling the ruins. A dystopia the shelf returns to across thirty years.

volumes.title: Incredible Hulk Omnibus
volumes.creators: Stan Lee, Jack Kirby & Steve Ditko
volumes.note: Where it starts. Six issues of the cancelled 1962 series, the whole Tales to Astonish run, and Hulk #102 picking the numbering back up.
volumes.lede: The book that failed, and then quietly worked out what it was in half the page count. Six issues, forty-odd Tales to Astonish chapters, and four different artists finding four different Hulks.
volumes.verdict: Universally treated as essential and rarely as anyone's favourite reading. The consensus is that the first six issues are historically fascinating and genuinely rough — the character is being invented in public — while the Tales to Astonish run is much better paced than its reputation and is where most readers say the book clicks.

volumes.title: Incredible Hulk Omnibus
volumes.creators: Stan Lee, Roy Thomas & Herb Trimpe
volumes.note: Trimpe becomes the definitive Bronze Age Hulk artist. Ka-Zar, the Rhino, the Leader's Humanoids and the first Sasquatch.
volumes.lede: Herb Trimpe takes the book and gives the character the look he will keep for a decade. This is where the 'classic' Hulk comic starts.
volumes.verdict: Well liked rather than argued about. The consistent line from readers is that Trimpe is the definitive Bronze Age Hulk artist, and this is where you watch him take ownership.

volumes.title: Incredible Hulk Omnibus
volumes.creators: Roy Thomas, Archie Goodwin & Herb Trimpe
volumes.note: Jarella, the Harpy, Doc Samson's debut and the Avengers #88 crossover that leads straight into Hulk #140.
volumes.lede: The Bronze Age proper: Jarella, the Harpy, Doc Samson, and a book that finally lets its lead be loved by somebody.
volumes.verdict: The most affectionately regarded of the four numbered volumes. Jarella in particular is the thing long-time readers bring up unprompted, and the Doc Samson debut is treated as one of the era's few genuinely durable additions.

volumes.title: Incredible Hulk Omnibus
volumes.creators: Len Wein, Roger Stern & Herb Trimpe
volumes.note: Ships February 2027 — it stays on the shelf ahead of that because its contents, its links and its jacket are all real. Hulk #180–181: the first Wolverine. Also the Bi-Beast, the Abomination's return, and issue #200.
volumes.lede: The end of Trimpe's run, the arrival of Len Wein and Roger Stern, and one eleven-page fight in the Canadian woods that changed the company.
volumes.verdict: Its reputation is dominated by #181, and slightly unfairly so — the issue's collector status has swallowed the discussion of everything around it. Readers who get past that tend to rate #200 and the late Stern issues as the strongest writing in any of the four numbered volumes.

volumes.title: Incredible Hulk by Peter David Omnibus
volumes.creators: Peter David, Todd McFarlane & Jeff Purves
volumes.note: The grey Hulk as Las Vegas leg-breaker Joe Fixit. Note the jump: Hulk #210–327 has never been collected in omnibus, so this opens 118 issues after Vol. 4 closes.
volumes.lede: The most abrupt tonal change on the shelf. The Hulk becomes grey, verbal, calculating and funny, moves to Las Vegas, and takes a job as a casino enforcer.
volumes.verdict: Fondly regarded, and usually recommended as the entry point to David's run rather than as its peak. The Joe Fixit material is the part people single out — it is unlike any other Hulk comic and it holds up.

volumes.title: Incredible Hulk by Peter David Omnibus
volumes.creators: Peter David, Dale Keown & Jeff Purves
volumes.note: Keown arrives and the Hulk is merged into the Professor. Ground Zero, the Pantheon, and issue #400.
volumes.lede: Dale Keown arrives, the personalities merge, and the run hits the stretch most readers name as its peak.
volumes.verdict: When readers argue about the best part of Peter David's twelve years, this is the stretch that wins most often. The combination of Keown's art at its height and the merged-Hulk premise arriving fresh is the reason.

volumes.title: Incredible Hulk by Peter David Omnibus
volumes.creators: Peter David, Gary Frank & George Pérez
volumes.note: Future Imperfect — the Maestro — plus the Troyjan War and Betty and Bruce finally married.
volumes.lede: Gary Frank makes the book quieter and better at acting, George Pérez shows up for two issues and steals the volume, and Bruce and Betty finally get married.
volumes.verdict: Future Imperfect is the reason this volume has the reputation it does. It is widely treated as a top-tier Hulk story and the Maestro as one of the few genuinely great late additions to the character's world; Pérez's art is singled out constantly.

volumes.title: Incredible Hulk by Peter David Omnibus
volumes.creators: Peter David, Angel Medina & Adam Kubert
volumes.note: The end of the twelve-year run: Onslaught, the Hulk split in two, and Banner alone.
volumes.lede: The 90s at full volume, a line-wide crossover machine reaching into the book, and the end of a twelve-year run.
volumes.verdict: Consistently rated the weakest of the four Peter David volumes, and the reasons given are usually external to David: crossover interference, a book being pulled into Onslaught and Heroes Reborn, and an art direction that has aged less well than Keown's or Frank's.

volumes.title: Hulk: Maestro by Peter David Omnibus
volumes.creators: Peter David, George Pérez & Germán Peralta
volumes.note: Every Maestro story in one book, so it doubles back over Future Imperfect and Hulk #460–461 from the volumes above — those issues share their ids, so marking them here marks them there.
volumes.lede: Thirty years of one idea: the Hulk who won, ruling the ruins of the world he helped end. Starts with a two-issue classic and follows the thread to the present.
volumes.verdict: Future Imperfect itself has an excellent reputation — commonly named alongside Planet Hulk and Immortal Hulk when people list the character's best stories, with Pérez's art doing much of the lifting.

volumes.title: Incredible Hulk by Byrne & Casey Omnibus
volumes.creators: John Byrne, Joe Casey & Ron Garney
volumes.note: The post-David relaunch: Byrne's short run, the retitled Hulk #1–11, and Rampaging Hulk.
volumes.lede: The awkward, interesting gap between two long runs: John Byrne relaunches the book, leaves in seven issues, and Joe Casey picks up the pieces.
volumes.verdict: Discussed mostly as a might-have-been. Byrne's Hulk has a small, persistent following who regard both his aborted runs as among the more interesting unrealised directions for the character, and the run has been described as a cult favourite on exactly those grounds.

volumes.title: Incredible Hulk: Return of the Monster Omnibus
volumes.creators: Bruce Jones, John Romita Jr. & Lee Weeks
volumes.note: Banner on the run, hunted by a conspiracy called Home Base. A thriller more than a superhero book, and the whole Bruce Jones run in one volume.
volumes.lede: The most formally radical book on the shelf, and the most argued about: a slow, cinematic conspiracy thriller that keeps the Hulk mostly off the page.
volumes.verdict: Genuinely split, and along a clean line. Readers who wanted a psychological thriller rate it very highly — the opening arc in particular is praised for atmosphere and for the nerve of keeping the Hulk off-panel. Readers who came for a Hulk comic frequently find it frustrating for exactly the same reason, and the phrase that recurs is that the smashing happens off-camera.

volumes.title: Incredible Hulk by Peter David Omnibus
volumes.creators: Peter David, Lee Weeks & Jae Lee
volumes.note: David's returns to the character, gathered rather than serialised: The End, the Tempest Fugit arc that follows Return of the Monster, and a long tail of one-shots.
chapters: Breaking Into Comics the Marvel Way! #2
volumes.lede: Not a run — a collection. Everything Peter David wrote about the Hulk after 1998, gathered rather than serialised, and it swings wildly in tone by design.
volumes.verdict: Reception tracks the contents. Hulk: The End is highly regarded — frequently named among the best single Hulk issues — and Tempest Fugit gets a warm, if not ecstatic, reception as a return to form after the Jones years.

volumes.title: Hulk: Planet Hulk Omnibus
volumes.creators: Greg Pak & Carlo Pagulayan
volumes.note: The Illuminati fire him into space and he lands on Sakaar. Gladiator, then king. The best-regarded Hulk story of the century so far.
volumes.lede: The best-regarded Hulk story of the century so far, and the one that proves the character works as a protagonist rather than a problem.
volumes.verdict: About as close to consensus as this shelf gets. It is routinely named the character's best modern story, sales on Incredible Hulk actually rose during it, and it is one of the very few Hulk arcs to be adapted twice — as an animated film and, in substance, as Thor: Ragnarok.

volumes.title: Hulk: World War Hulk Omnibus
volumes.creators: Greg Pak & John Romita Jr.
volumes.note: He comes back for the Illuminati. The core series plus every tie-in and the whole Aftersmash line, each mini as its own chapter.
volumes.lede: He comes home for the people who exiled him. The rarest configuration in the character's history: the Hulk as the aggressor, and the reader on his side.
volumes.verdict: Regarded as a rare event that delivers what it promises, and as the proper payoff to Planet Hulk rather than a cash-in. Romita Jr.'s art and the moral inversion are the two things praised most consistently.

volumes.title: Hulk by Loeb & McGuinness Omnibus
volumes.creators: Jeph Loeb & Ed McGuinness
volumes.note: The Red Hulk mystery and the Hulk (2008) ongoing. Loud, and the whodunit is the point.
volumes.lede: A red Hulk, a year-long whodunit, and some of the loudest, most unembarrassed superhero art of its decade. The shelf's biggest gap between commercial success and critical standing.
volumes.verdict: The most negatively received book on this shelf, though 'panned' overstates it — the reception is sharply split rather than uniform. The recurring criticisms are that the plotting is thin and predictable, that the book felt rudderless until the Red Hulk's identity was revealed, and that the character is written so over-powered that the fights stop having stakes.

volumes.title: Immortal Hulk Omnibus
volumes.creators: Al Ewing & Joe Bennett
volumes.note: All 50 issues plus #0 and the tie-ins. A horror book about what the Hulk actually is — the run that reframed the character.
volumes.lede: Horror, taken literally. The run that reframed the character and the best-reviewed Hulk comic since Peter David.
volumes.verdict: Very widely held to be the best Hulk run since Peter David, with multiple Eisner-winning issues, and credited with making the character frightening again after a decade of blockbuster treatment. It has also changed how the older books read — a lot of readers go back to 1962 after this and find it much more of a horror comic than they remembered.

volumes.title: Hulk by Cates & Ottley Omnibus
volumes.creators: Donny Cates & Ryan Ottley
volumes.note: Banner pilots the Hulk like a ship. Runs straight into Banner of War, which is why the two Thor issues sit between Hulk #6 and #8.
chapters: Hulk vs. Thor: Banner of War Alpha #1
volumes.lede: A hard swerve away from horror into loud science fiction: Banner has turned his own body into a spacecraft and is flying it.
volumes.verdict: The most argued-about recent book on the shelf. The art is close to universally praised — readers who dislike the run still rate Ottley's work on it highly.

tone_modes.label: Most foundational
tone_modes.description: The Hulk debut, the Claremont/Miller miniseries, and Weapon X in one volume. Everything the character is was decided in these pages.

tone_modes.label: Most genre
tone_modes.description: Madripoor — a white suit, an eyepatch and a pirate port. Casablanca with claws, and completely unlike the X-Men book it spun out of.

tone_modes.label: Most 1990s
tone_modes.description: Silvestri and Kubert, cross-hatching, hologram covers, and the three years he had bone claws and was dying. The decade at full volume.

tone_modes.label: Most crime fiction
tone_modes.description: Ellis and Yu in Hong Kong. Two timeframes, a hitman, almost no superheroes. Four issues and nothing wasted.

tone_modes.label: Most action
tone_modes.description: Enemy of the State — brainwashed and pointed at the Marvel Universe, and winning. Romita Jr. at full throttle.

tone_modes.label: Most western
tone_modes.description: Old Man Logan. Fifty years after the villains won, an old pacifist driving across a ruined America. Openly Unforgiven.

tone_modes.label: Darkest
tone_modes.description: Aaron's southern gothic — revenge, damnation, and a trip to Hell that is not a metaphor.

tone_modes.label: Best written
tone_modes.description: Uncanny X-Force. A book about people who decided to kill for the greater good and are being destroyed by it. The one to read if you read one.

tone_modes.label: Most elegiac
tone_modes.description: Losing the healing factor and dying slowly, treated as a last ride rather than a battle.

volumes.title: Wolverine Omnibus
volumes.creators: Chris Claremont, Frank Miller & Barry Windsor-Smith
volumes.note: Opens on Weapon X rather than on his first appearance — the book puts the origin first and then goes back to Incredible Hulk #180. Everything that made him: the Claremont/Miller miniseries, Kitty Pryde and Wolverine, and the first ten issues of the solo ongoing.
volumes.lede: The three foundational texts in one book: the Hulk debut, the Claremont/Miller miniseries, and Weapon X. Almost nothing about the character was decided outside these pages.
volumes.verdict: The one volume on this shelf nobody argues about. It holds three separate landmark stories — the debut, the miniseries and Weapon X — any of which would justify a book.

volumes.title: Wolverine Omnibus
volumes.creators: Chris Claremont, John Buscema & Peter David
volumes.note: Madripoor, and Logan working as Patch. The brown-and-tan run at full strength, with thirty-four Marvel Comics Presents chapters threaded through it and Havok and Wolverine: Meltdown as the odd painted one out.
volumes.lede: The solo ongoing starts, and the best decision in it is the setting: a fictional pirate port where he wears a white suit and an eyepatch and calls himself Patch.
volumes.verdict: Quietly well liked and much less discussed than what surrounds it. Readers who rate it point at Madripoor and at the genre confidence — it is the only stretch where the solo book has a wholly distinct identity.

volumes.title: Wolverine Omnibus
volumes.creators: Larry Hama, Marc Silvestri & Peter David
volumes.note: Hama takes over and holds the book for the next eight years. Silvestri draws it, Hearts of Darkness pairs him with Ghost Rider and the Punisher, and the Marvel Comics Presents run reaches #108.
volumes.lede: Larry Hama arrives and Marc Silvestri defines what Wolverine looks like for a decade.
volumes.verdict: Hama's run is described by a lot of long-time readers as definitive, and this is where it starts working. The combination with Silvestri is the specific thing people name.

volumes.title: Wolverine Omnibus
volumes.creators: Larry Hama, Marc Silvestri & Mark Texeira
volumes.note: Runs to #75 — Fatal Attractions, where Magneto pulls the adamantium out through his skin and the character stops being indestructible. Sabretooth's first solo miniseries is here too.
chapters: Wolverine and the Punisher: Damaging Evidence #1–3
volumes.lede: The adamantium comes out. Three years of a Wolverine with bone claws who is slowly dying — the boldest thing anyone has done to him.
volumes.verdict: The adamantium removal is generally rated as the best structural idea of the 90s Wolverine, precisely because it took away the thing that made him unbeatable and forced the writing to compensate.

volumes.title: Wolverine Omnibus
volumes.creators: Larry Hama, Adam Kubert & Val Semeiks
volumes.note: Bone claws, and a body that is slowly failing without the metal. Hama writes the devolution the whole way down, through #100 and the Genesis story, with a tail of mid-nineties one-shots after it.
volumes.lede: The bone-claw years at full stretch, Adam Kubert on art, and a run that goes considerably stranger than its reputation.
volumes.verdict: Splits on the feral direction. Its defenders argue it is the honest consequence of removing the adamantium and that Kubert's art is the best on the whole Hama run; its detractors find the devolution a step too far and the period excesses hard going.

volumes.title: Wolverine Omnibus
volumes.creators: Larry Hama, Val Semeiks & Anthony Winn
volumes.note: Onslaught, the feral turn, and the end of Hama's run. Ends up more anthology than ongoing — Days of Future Past, Ben Grimm and Logan, Kitty Pryde: Agent of S.H.I.E.L.D. and the two-issue Wolverine Encyclopedia all sit alongside the main title.
chapters: Before the Fantastic Four: Ben Grimm and Logan #1–3
volumes.lede: The end of Hama's seven years, and the adamantium comes back.
volumes.verdict: Consistently rated last among the numbered volumes. The reasons are ordinary — a long run running down, crossover interference, and an art team readers rate below Silvestri and Kubert.

volumes.title: Wolverine: Not Dead Yet Omnibus
volumes.creators: Warren Ellis, Erik Larsen & Leinil Francis Yu
volumes.note: Named for the four-issue Ellis and Yu story that is the best thing in it. Picks up at #119 and runs to #158, and that is where the shelf stops — #159–189 is uncollected until The Return of Weapon X Omnibus prints it in 2027. Only #175, the anniversary issue, escapes the gap, in the Jason Aaron volume.
volumes.lede: Warren Ellis writes four issues of crime fiction and they are better than most of the hundred around them.
volumes.verdict: Not Dead Yet itself is very well regarded and turns up on best-of lists regularly — a tight crime story with no fat on it, and Yu's breakout.

volumes.title: Wolverine by Mark Millar Omnibus
volumes.creators: Mark Millar, John Romita Jr. & Steve McNiven
volumes.note: Two runs in one book. Enemy of the State turns him into HYDRA's weapon and points him at everyone he knows; Old Man Logan, five years later, is the western about the version of him who quit — those seven issues are in the Old Man Logan omnibus too, which is where the overlap pill on them comes from.
volumes.lede: Two high-concept swings, both of which escaped into the wider culture: brainwashed and aimed at the Marvel Universe, then an old man in a ruined America.
volumes.verdict: Both stories are among the best-known Wolverine comics of the century. Old Man Logan in particular has had enormous reach — it supplied the shape of the Logan film and has spawned an ongoing series and multiple sequels.

volumes.title: Wolverine by Jason Aaron Omnibus
volumes.creators: Jason Aaron, Ron Garney & Adam Kubert
volumes.note: Get Mystique, Manifest Destiny, and all sixteen issues of Wolverine: Weapon X — the run where Aaron works out that the character is funniest and worst when he is certain he deserves what is coming.
volumes.lede: Southern gothic: revenge, damnation, and a lead who knows exactly where he is going when he dies.
volumes.verdict: Well regarded and slightly overshadowed by Aaron's later, louder work. Get Mystique is the part readers name, and the Garney art on it gets consistent praise.

volumes.title: Wolverine Goes to Hell Omnibus
volumes.creators: Jason Aaron, Renato Guedes & Jason Latour
volumes.note: Aaron's second stretch: his soul in Hell, his body driving around murdering people, and Schism at the end of it — the argument with Cyclops that splits the X-Men in two.
volumes.lede: The title is not a metaphor. His body is possessed and his soul is in Hell, and the book runs both threads at once.
volumes.verdict: Splits on the premise. Readers who enjoy Aaron's willingness to go big rate it as the boldest modern Wolverine run; readers who want street-level Logan find the demons a step too far.

volumes.title: Uncanny X-Force by Rick Remender Omnibus
volumes.creators: Rick Remender, Jerome Opeña & Esad Ribić
volumes.note: Wolverine's black-ops team, and the best-regarded X-book of its decade. The Apocalypse Solution, Dark Angel Saga and The Final Execution, the whole run. Shares its Road to Hell prologue with Goes to Hell, so that issue carries the same id in both.
volumes.lede: A team book, on this shelf because it is Logan's team — and by common consent one of the best Marvel runs of its decade.
volumes.verdict: Very widely rated one of the best Marvel runs of the 2010s, and the single most enthusiastically recommended book on this shelf after the first volume.

volumes.title: Death of Wolverine Omnibus
volumes.creators: Paul Cornell, Charles Soule & Steve McNiven
volumes.note: Cornell strips the healing factor, Soule spends four issues killing him, and the tie-ins deal with the hole it leaves. He goes out encased in the metal he spent forty years being defined by.
chapters: Death of Wolverine: The Weapon X Program #1–5
Death of Wolverine: The Logan Legacy #1–7
Death of Wolverine: Deadpool & Captain America #1
Death of Wolverine: Life After Logan #1
volumes.lede: They take the healing factor away and let him die slowly. It is a last ride rather than a final battle, and it stuck for four years.
volumes.verdict: Received as a well-made send-off that did the difficult thing: made a death everyone knew would be undone feel like it mattered while you were reading it. McNiven's art is singled out.

volumes.title: Wolverine: Old Man Logan Omnibus
volumes.creators: Mark Millar, Jeff Lemire & Andrea Sorrentino
volumes.note: Ships 15 December 2026 — on the shelf ahead of that because its contents, links and jacket are all real. Millar and McNiven's original story is here again (the Millar volume has it too, so those seven issues carry the overlap pill), and then the part that was missing: Lemire and Sorrentino's ongoing, which drops the old man into the present day and lets him try to stop his own future from happening.
volumes.lede: The original story plus the ongoing series that grew out of it — the old Logan pulled into the present day, still carrying what he did.
volumes.standing: Strong, and the sequel is the surprise
volumes.verdict: The original story is a modern classic. What people are consistently surprised by is the Lemire and Sorrentino ongoing, which had every reason to be a cash-in and is instead one of the best-looking Marvel books of the 2010s.

volumes.title: Return of Wolverine Omnibus
volumes.creators: Charles Soule, Ray-Anthony Height & Declan Shalvey
volumes.note: Four years of everyone else looking for him: Wolverines, the five Hunt for Wolverine minis, the Marvel Legacy one-shot that gave it away, and finally the return itself.
chapters: Hunt for Wolverine: Claws of a Killer #1–4
Hunt for Wolverine: Mystery in Madripoor #1–4
volumes.lede: The four years he was gone, and the story that brought him back.
volumes.verdict: The consensus is that the absence was handled better than the return. The material about a world without him gets real credit; the resurrection story itself is widely described as underwhelming and mechanically fussy.

volumes.title: Wolverine: Sabretooth War Omnibus
volumes.creators: Victor LaValle, Benjamin Percy & Geoff Shaw
volumes.note: The oldest fight on the shelf, finished. LaValle's two Sabretooth minis set it up and Percy's Wolverine #41–50 pays it off — the shortest book here and the only one that is a single story.
volumes.lede: Fifty years of the one relationship the character has never resolved, finally addressed.
volumes.verdict: Too recent for a settled verdict, but the reception has been positive, with LaValle's Sabretooth singled out as considerably more ambitious than a tie-in mini needed to be.

tone_modes.label: Most pulp
tone_modes.description: The 1970s and the early solo run — multiple identities as a tactic borrowed from The Shadow, not as a diagnosis. Adventure, not horror.

tone_modes.label: Best art on the shelf
tone_modes.description: Sienkiewicz turning into himself in public, monthly, over three years. If you read this shelf for one reason, make it this.

tone_modes.label: Most 1990s
tone_modes.description: Sixty issues of straight-ahead action, and then Stephen Platt rendering every surface in the book. A period document.

tone_modes.label: Most violent
tone_modes.description: Huston and Finch. A man who is genuinely unwell, a god who looks like a corpse, and consequences that stay on the page.

tone_modes.label: Best written
tone_modes.description: Ellis and Shalvey: six standalone issues in six registers, and the white suit. An hour to read and the best hour on the shelf.

tone_modes.label: Warmest
tone_modes.description: MacKay's Midnight Mission — a clinic, a congregation, and a character with something to do other than suffer. Funny without losing the horror.

volumes.title: Moon Knight Omnibus
volumes.creators: Doug Moench, Don Perlin & Bill Sienkiewicz
volumes.note: Everything before he had his own book, then the book. A two-issue hired thug in Werewolf by Night, a Defenders villain, a Hulk! magazine serial where Sienkiewicz worked the look out in black and white — and then Moon Knight #1–20, which is where Moench and Sienkiewicz stop imitating Batman and start doing the thing about four men in one head.
volumes.lede: From a werewolf comic to his own title, and a nineteen-year-old artist starting a transformation you can watch happen page by page.
volumes.verdict: Well regarded, and the near-universal reason given is Sienkiewicz. The Moench scripts are solid 1970s Marvel — competent, a bit wordy, unremarkable — and the art is the event.

volumes.title: Moon Knight Omnibus
volumes.creators: Doug Moench, Bill Sienkiewicz & Kevin Nowlan
volumes.note: The end of the original run and the first attempt to restart it. Morpheus, Stained Glass Scarlet and Black Spectre close out #21–38; Fist of Khonshu revives him in 1985 for six issues and does not take. The rest is guest spots — Iron Man, Power Man and Iron Fist, three Marvel Fanfares — and a handful of Marvel Age pieces about the two relaunches.
volumes.lede: The end of the original run at Sienkiewicz's peak, the Fist of Khonshu revival, and a long tail of guest appearances.
volumes.verdict: The Sienkiewicz issues are the best-regarded material on this shelf and are frequently cited well outside Moon Knight discussion as a landmark of American comics art.

volumes.title: Moon Knight: Marc Spector Omnibus
volumes.creators: Chuck Dixon, Sal Velluto & Ron Garney
volumes.note: His longest-running title, sixty issues of it, and this is the first thirty-four. Dixon puts him back on the street and then back in Burunda against Bushman, and the volume ends inside Round Robin — six issues of Amazing Spider-Man where he, Spidey and the Punisher are all chasing the same frame-up.
volumes.lede: Sixty issues of straight-ahead action begin. Chuck Dixon writes him as a competent professional with a supporting cast — no illness, no ambiguity.
volumes.verdict: Liked by the readers who have got to it and rarely discussed. The consistent assessment is well-made, unpretentious action comics — Dixon at his most dependable.

volumes.title: Moon Knight: Marc Spector Omnibus
volumes.creators: Terry Kavanagh, Ron Garney & Stephen Platt
volumes.note: #35–60 and then the wilderness. Infinity War, the Punisher, Doctor Doom, and the Platt issues that briefly made this the hottest-drawn book at Marvel. After it folds he only surfaces in fours: Resurrection War in 1998, High Strangeness in 1999, and Priest's Black Panther in 2000.
volumes.lede: The back half, and the decade catches up hard — including the shelf's clearest artefact of a 1990s art fashion.
volumes.verdict: The most divided volume on this small shelf. Readers with affection for early-90s art rate the Platt issues highly; readers without it find them close to unreadable, and the crossover material has few defenders anywhere.

volumes.title: Moon Knight by Huston, Benson & Hurwitz Omnibus
volumes.creators: Charlie Huston, David Finch & Mike Benson
volumes.note: The 2006 relaunch, which is the one that decided he was horror rather than crime. Huston opens with a cripple in a wheelchair talking to a corpse; Benson and then Hurwitz push it further; Vengeance of the Moon Knight walks him back toward being a hero, and Shadowland takes it away again.
volumes.lede: A crime novelist takes the book and makes it the most violent version there has been — and the first to treat the identities as illness rather than tactic.
volumes.verdict: Well regarded and genuinely consequential: this is where the modern reading of the character starts, and everything since — Ellis, Lemire, MacKay — is in conversation with it.

volumes.title: Moon Knight: From The Dead Omnibus
volumes.creators: Warren Ellis, Declan Shalvey & Brian Wood
volumes.note: Seventeen issues, nearly all done-in-one. Ellis and Shalvey's first six are the ones people mean — the white suit, the sharp tailoring, and a page grammar the book never really got back after they left. Note the jump to get here: Bendis and Maleev's 2011 series has never been collected in omnibus.
volumes.lede: Six issues, six self-contained stories, six different registers, and the white suit. The best hour on this shelf.
volumes.verdict: The Ellis and Shalvey six issues are the most recommended Moon Knight comics there are, and readers describe them as a substantial improvement on everything immediately around them. The white-suit design has been kept by nearly every version since, including on screen.

volumes.title: Moon Knight by Jed MacKay Omnibus
volumes.creators: Jed MacKay, Alessandro Cappuccio & Federico Sabbatini
volumes.note: The Midnight Mission — Marc running a walk-in shelter for people the weird has come for, and thirty issues of the argument about whether that counts as atonement. All of MacKay's run, both annuals and the Devil's Reign tie-in. Lemire's 2016 series and Bemis's after it are the gap in front of it; neither has an omnibus.
volumes.lede: He opens a walk-in clinic. The first version of this character that is about service rather than suffering, and the funniest book on the shelf.
volumes.verdict: Strong reception throughout its run and treated as one of the better recent Marvel books. The specific praise is for the Midnight Mission premise — giving the character a function instead of a condition — and for the balance of horror and humour.

tone_modes.label: Lightest
tone_modes.description: The Silver Age book: wisecracks, bright colours, a hero who is having a reasonably good time. Read for Wally Wood's costume and Gene Colan's camera.

tone_modes.label: Most 1970s
tone_modes.description: San Francisco, the Black Widow, relationship drama and a hero with no fixed city. The furthest the character has ever been from Hell's Kitchen.

tone_modes.label: Most influential
tone_modes.description: Miller and Janson. Crime fiction, ninjas, the Kingpin promoted to a monster, and Elektra. Everything after this is a response to it.

tone_modes.label: Best single story
tone_modes.description: Born Again, in the Companion. Karen Page sells his name and the Kingpin takes his life apart without throwing a punch. Frequently named the best superhero story ever written.

tone_modes.label: Strangest
tone_modes.description: Nocenti's run — political, surreal, argumentative, and a trip to Hell. Nothing else on any shelf here reads like it.

tone_modes.label: Most crime novel
tone_modes.description: Bendis and Maleev, then Brubaker and Lark. Long arcs, almost no superheroics, and a secret identity that is public.

tone_modes.label: Darkest
tone_modes.description: Shadowland — the end of the spiral, and the book at its least fun. Read it to understand why the next run is bright.

tone_modes.label: Brightest
tone_modes.description: Waid, Rivera and Samnee. Primary colours, adventure plotting, and the best visual solution anyone has found for the radar sense.

tone_modes.label: Most Catholic
tone_modes.description: Zdarsky. Guilt, confession, a man who kills someone and cannot forgive himself for it. The best-reviewed run since Bendis.

volumes.title: Daredevil Omnibus
volumes.creators: Stan Lee, Wally Wood & Gene Colan
volumes.note: The yellow suit, and then the red one. Bill Everett draws #1 and vanishes; Wally Wood arrives at #5, redesigns the costume into the thing everyone pictures, and leaves by #11. What holds it together is Gene Colan from #20 on — a fluid, cinematic pencil nobody else at Marvel had, and the reason this run outlived its own scripts.
volumes.lede: The yellow suit, then the red one. A book that does not yet know what it is, rescued twice by artists.
volumes.verdict: Rated well below the Silver Age Spider-Man and Fantastic Four books it was made alongside, and few readers pretend otherwise. The stories are formulaic, and the Mike Murdock material is the single most-mocked thing in the character's history.

volumes.title: Daredevil Omnibus
volumes.creators: Roy Thomas, Gene Colan & Barry Windsor-Smith
volumes.note: Colan's run at full stretch. The Jester frames Matt for murder, Starr Saxon works out who he is, and the book spends an embarrassing stretch on the Mike Murdock twin-brother lie before killing it off. Roy Thomas takes over the scripts; the two Iron Man issues at the end are the Zodiac crossover.
volumes.lede: Colan at full stretch, Roy Thomas on scripts, and the book finally killing off its worst idea.
volumes.verdict: Consistently rated a step up: the scripts get better, the Colan art gets considerably better, and the book starts to have real antagonists.

volumes.title: Daredevil Omnibus
volumes.creators: Gerry Conway, Steve Gerber & Gene Colan
volumes.note: Daredevil and the Black Widow, which is what the cover said for four years — Matt leaves New York for San Francisco and the book becomes a two-hander. Natasha's own Amazing Adventures strips are collected in front of it, so you get her solo run and the partnership it fed into.
volumes.lede: Daredevil and the Black Widow. Matt leaves New York for San Francisco and the book becomes a two-hander — the furthest the character has ever strayed.
volumes.verdict: Divides readers along an unusual line: people who came to Daredevil through Miller find it almost unrecognisable, and people who like 1970s Marvel for its own sake rate it well.

volumes.title: Daredevil Omnibus
volumes.creators: Marv Wolfman, Jim Shooter & Gene Colan
volumes.note: Ships September 2026 — on the shelf ahead of that because its contents, links and jacket are all real. The stretch nobody collects: Matt back in New York, Bullseye created, the Death-Stalker and the Purple Man, and Klaus Janson arriving as inker two issues before the book changes forever. It ends on #158, Frank Miller's first issue, which the Miller & Janson volume then opens with.
volumes.lede: The stretch nobody collects: back to New York, Bullseye created, and Klaus Janson arriving two issues before everything changes.
volumes.verdict: The least-discussed volume on the shelf and the one most readers buy for position rather than content: it fills the gap between the Black Widow years and Miller, and it holds Bullseye's debut.

volumes.title: Daredevil by Miller & Janson Omnibus
volumes.creators: Frank Miller, Klaus Janson & Roger McKenzie
volumes.note: The run that decided what Daredevil is. Miller arrives as the artist on #158 under Roger McKenzie, takes the writing at #168 with Elektra, and by the time he leaves at #191 the book is about Hell's Kitchen, the Hand, and Wilson Fisk. #162 is skipped because it is a Ditko fill-in, not theirs. Note it opens on #158, which Omnibus Vol. 4 also holds — that issue is Miller's first and both books want it, so it is the shelf's only overlap.
volumes.lede: The run that decided what Daredevil is. A twenty-two-year-old artist turns a failing superhero book into a crime comic, and the character never goes back.
volumes.verdict: One of the small handful of runs that changed what mainstream comics could be, and its influence is everywhere — on Daredevil obviously, but also on the entire 1980s turn toward crime and noir in superhero books.

volumes.title: Daredevil by Frank Miller Omnibus Companion
volumes.creators: Frank Miller, David Mazzucchelli & John Romita Jr.
volumes.note: Everything Miller wrote about Matt without also drawing the monthly. The centre of it is Born Again — Karen Page sells his identity for a fix and Fisk takes him apart piece by piece — which is the best eight issues anyone has done with this character. Around it: Love and War, the Man Without Fear origin mini with Romita Jr., and two early Spectacular Spider-Man crossovers.
volumes.lede: Everything Miller wrote about Matt Murdock without also drawing the monthly — including Born Again, which is the best of it and arguably the best of anything.
volumes.verdict: Born Again is very frequently named the greatest superhero story ever written, and when it is not, it is on the shortlist. The specific praise is for the Kingpin — a villain who wins by paperwork — and for Mazzucchelli, whose work here is treated as a high point of the medium.

volumes.title: Daredevil by Nocenti & Romita Jr. Omnibus
volumes.creators: Ann Nocenti & John Romita Jr.
volumes.note: Nocenti picks the book up straight out of Born Again and takes it somewhere nobody expected — Inferno, Mephisto, the Kingpin's factory towns, and a running argument about what a blind Catholic lawyer is doing punching people. Typhoid Mary arrives at #254. Daredevil #192–218 and #220–225, the Denny O'Neil run in between, has never been omnibused.
volumes.lede: The impossible job — following Born Again — answered by refusing to compete and going somewhere much stranger.
volumes.verdict: Long overshadowed by what precedes it and steadily reappraised upward. The consistent modern line is that Nocenti's run is far more ambitious than it was given credit for — political, formally odd, and unwilling to repeat Miller.

volumes.title: Daredevil by Nocenti & Romita Jr. Omnibus
volumes.creators: Ann Nocenti, John Romita Jr. & Lee Weeks
volumes.note: The back half, and it gets stranger — Matt loses the costume, the memory and most of the supporting cast, and the run ends up in Hell with Mephisto. The tail is the Marvel Comics Presents backups Nocenti kept writing afterwards, plus two Spectacular Spider-Man issues and a Christmas story.
volumes.lede: The back half, and it gets much stranger — Matt loses the costume, the memory and most of the cast, and the run ends in Hell.
volumes.verdict: Splits harder than Vol. 1. Its admirers call it one of the most genuinely experimental mainstream superhero runs of its decade; its detractors call it self-indulgent and say the book stopped being about anything.

volumes.title: Daredevil by Brian Michael Bendis Omnibus
volumes.creators: Brian Michael Bendis & Alex Maleev
volumes.note: Bendis and Maleev do crime fiction: a tabloid prints Matt's name on the front page in #32 and the next fifty issues are about living with that. Only the Bendis issues are here, so #20–25 (Bob Gale) and #51–55 (David Mack's Echo) are skipped. Getting here means jumping Daredevil #292–380 and the whole Marvel Knights relaunch by Kevin Smith and Mack — none of it has an omnibus.
volumes.lede: A tabloid prints Matt Murdock's name on the front page, and the most influential modern run begins.
volumes.verdict: Eisner-winning, enormously influential, and generally treated as the definitive modern Daredevil alongside Miller's. It is the run the Netflix series took most of its texture from.

volumes.title: Daredevil by Brian Michael Bendis Omnibus
volumes.creators: Brian Michael Bendis & Alex Maleev
volumes.note: Matt declares himself Kingpin of Hell's Kitchen, marries Milla Donovan, and ends the run in a federal prison cell. The Eisner-winning half. Three Ultimate Marvel Team-Up issues and a What If about Karen Page surviving Bendis's own best-known scene are collected after it.
chapters: What If Karen Page Had Lived? #1
volumes.lede: The back half: the consequences of the outing, the Kingpin's fall, and an ending that leaves the character somewhere no writer had left him before.
volumes.verdict: Rated alongside Vol. 1 and by some readers above it, on the grounds that the consequences are more interesting than the premise and that the run commits to them.

volumes.title: Daredevil by Ed Brubaker Omnibus
volumes.creators: Ed Brubaker & Michael Lark
volumes.note: Brubaker and Lark pick the book up mid-sentence with Matt in Ryker's, which is the best possible way to inherit a run this good. The Devil in Cell-Block D, then Europe, then back to a Hell's Kitchen that has moved on without him. Lark's storytelling is tighter than Maleev's and the book loses nothing.
volumes.lede: The handover that does not reset. Brubaker inherits a protagonist in prison and writes him out slowly, in the best pure crime writing the book has had.
volumes.verdict: Very well regarded and slightly under-celebrated, largely because it sits between two runs with louder reputations. The prison material is the part readers name, and Brubaker's refusal to hit reset is what gets the specific credit.

volumes.title: Daredevil by Ed Brubaker Omnibus
volumes.creators: Ed Brubaker, Michael Lark & Greg Rucka
volumes.note: Lady Bullseye, Master Izo, and the long slide that puts the Hand's offer in front of Matt at exactly the moment he has nothing left to say no with. Ends on #500 and the decision that starts Shadowland.
volumes.lede: The end of the crime decade, and the run that walks the character to the edge of Shadowland.
volumes.verdict: Well regarded, and generally rated a shade below Vol. 1 — the recurring note is that the relentless downward pressure gets wearing across two omnibuses of it.

volumes.title: Daredevil: Shadowland Omnibus
volumes.creators: Andy Diggle, Antony Johnston & Roberto De La Torre
volumes.note: Matt takes the Hand, builds a fortress on top of Hell's Kitchen and kills Bullseye in it. The whole event with every tie-in — Elektra, Ghost Rider, Spider-Man, Moon Knight, Power Man, Blood on the Streets — plus the Diggle run that leads in and Daredevil: Reborn, which is Matt walking out into New Mexico afterwards to work out whether he is still worth anything.
volumes.lede: The end of the spiral. Matt takes over the Hand, builds a fortress in Hell's Kitchen, and starts killing — and the readership decided it had gone far enough.
volumes.verdict: The most disliked book on this shelf, and the criticisms are consistent and specific: the heel turn is not earned — Matt goes from compromised to murderous without the story showing the step — the plot jumps between disconnected events, and several tie-in threads (an extended Moon Knight setup among them) go nowhere at all.

volumes.title: Daredevil by Mark Waid Omnibus
volumes.creators: Mark Waid, Paolo Rivera & Marcos Martín
volumes.note: The tonal reset, and the reason it worked: Waid stops writing a man in a permanent depressive episode and starts writing a man performing not being in one. Rivera and Martín render the radar sense as something beautiful rather than something grim. The Omega Drive arc brings in Spider-Man and the Punisher.
volumes.lede: Somebody turns the lights on. Primary colours, adventure plotting, a Matt Murdock who smiles — and it is much sadder underneath than it looks.
volumes.verdict: Eisner-winning and very widely loved. The consistent line is that it rescued the character from a decade of diminishing returns, and that it did so without pretending the decade had not happened.

volumes.title: Daredevil by Mark Waid Omnibus
volumes.creators: Mark Waid & Chris Samnee
volumes.note: Samnee takes over and the book wins an Eisner for it. Foggy's cancer, the Sons of the Serpent, the identity finally becoming public on Matt's own terms, and then the move to San Francisco for the 2014 relaunch — the second time this character has answered a bad year by leaving New York.
volumes.lede: The back half, with Samnee as a full co-storyteller, and a relocation to San Francisco that is the shelf's second-best joke.
volumes.verdict: Rated alongside Vol. 1 and, for the Samnee art, sometimes above it. The Waid–Samnee partnership is treated as one of the best writer/artist pairings of the 2010s at Marvel.

volumes.title: Daredevil by Charles Soule Omnibus
volumes.creators: Charles Soule, Ron Garney & Goran Sudžuka
volumes.note: Soule is a lawyer, and it shows — this is the run that takes the day job seriously, with Matt as an ADA prosecuting the people he used to punch. Garney's black-and-red art strips the palette down to almost nothing. Runs from the 2015 relaunch through the renumbering back to #595 and out at #612.
volumes.lede: The only run written by someone who actually practises law, and the one that puts Matt on the other side of the courtroom.
volumes.verdict: Caught between two very well-liked runs and correspondingly under-discussed. Readers who rate it highly point at the legal material, which is the best-informed version of it the character has had.

volumes.title: Daredevil by Chip Zdarsky Omnibus
volumes.creators: Chip Zdarsky, Marco Checchetto & Jorge Fornés
volumes.note: Matt kills a man in the second issue and the next fifty are the sentence. Zdarsky and Checchetto write the best long-form Daredevil since Bendis: prison, Elektra taking the costume, Fisk as mayor of New York, and a book that keeps insisting the Catholic guilt was always the point rather than the decoration.
volumes.lede: The best-reviewed Daredevil since Bendis. It opens with Matt killing someone by accident and spends years refusing to let him off.
volumes.verdict: Very widely rated the best Daredevil run since Bendis and Maleev, with Eisner nominations for Zdarsky as writer and for the series. The specific praise is for taking the religion seriously and for a premise that is allowed to have real consequences.

volumes.title: Daredevil by Chip Zdarsky Omnibus
volumes.creators: Chip Zdarsky, Marco Checchetto & Rafael De Latorre
volumes.note: The end of it. Devil's Reign is here in full — Fisk outlawing costumed heroes from City Hall — and then the 2022 relaunch, where Matt and Elektra run a Hand of their own and the run walks itself into the ending it has been aiming at since the first issue. Woman Without Fear is Elektra's half of the same story.
volumes.lede: The conclusion — Devil's Reign, the Fist, and an ending that goes further than any previous run dared.
volumes.verdict: Well received, and generally rated a step below Vol. 1 for the same reason second halves usually are: the setup was more distinctive than the payoff, and the scale goes up in ways that pull against the intimate register that made the run's reputation.

tone_modes.label: Most philosophical
tone_modes.description: Lee and Buscema, 1968. Soliloquies about human cruelty from a man who cannot leave. Stan Lee's most personal work, and the most beautiful figure drawing on the shelf.

tone_modes.label: Most space opera
tone_modes.description: The 1987 relaunch with the barrier gone — Kree, Skrulls, galactic politics. Plus Moebius's Parable, which looks like nothing else Marvel has printed.

tone_modes.label: Most consequential
tone_modes.description: Starlin's Thanos material. The Surfer's own title becomes the launchpad for the biggest event in Marvel's history — at the cost of being about him.

tone_modes.label: Happiest
tone_modes.description: Slott and Allred. Doctor Who with a surfboard, in flat pop-art colour, and an Eisner-winning issue that reads upside down. The only joyful book here.

volumes.title: Silver Surfer Omnibus
volumes.creators: Stan Lee & John Buscema
volumes.note: The Lee and Buscema book, and still the one the character is measured against. Eighteen issues of Galactus's herald marooned inside a barrier over Earth, being magnificent about it and miserable about it in the same panel. It opens with the Fantastic Four Annual where he first got a story of his own, and closes on the Not Brand Echh parody, which is what happened to anything Marvel took seriously in 1969.
volumes.lede: Eighteen double-sized issues of Stan Lee's most personal writing, drawn by John Buscema at the height of his powers — and cancelled anyway.
volumes.verdict: The art has no detractors. Buscema's work here is routinely named among the finest of the Silver Age, and the double-sized format is a large part of why.

volumes.title: Silver Surfer: Return to the Spaceways Omnibus
volumes.creators: Steve Englehart, Marshall Rogers & Ron Lim
volumes.note: The barrier breaks and he goes back to the stars. A Stan Lee and John Byrne one-shot in 1982, then Englehart and Rogers relaunch him in 1987 for thirty-three issues — the Kree/Skrull war restarted, the Elders of the Universe hunting Galactus, Nova and Mantis and Shalla-Bal. The tail of the book is the odd material: both of Stan Lee's graphic novels, Moebius drawing Parable, Epic Illustrated #1 and the first Marvel Comics Presents. Note the jump to get here — he had no title at all between 1970 and 1982.
volumes.lede: The barrier comes down and the book becomes space opera at last — plus two graphic novels and Moebius.
volumes.verdict: Well regarded, and the reception is unusually split by component. Englehart's relaunch is treated as the moment the character finally worked as an ongoing concern. Parable is regarded as an art landmark and gets recommended well outside superhero circles.

volumes.title: Silver Surfer: The Infinity Gauntlet Omnibus
volumes.creators: Jim Starlin, Ron Marz & Ron Lim
volumes.note: Ships 3 November 2026 — it is on the shelf ahead of that because its contents, its links and its jacket are all real, which is the bar a tile has to clear. Starlin takes the book over at #34 and it stops being a story about the Surfer's conscience and becomes a story about Thanos. The Thanos Quest collects the six stones, Infinity Gauntlet spends them, and the Surfer's own title runs alongside the whole thing to #66 — which is the argument for reading the crossover here, in his book, rather than on its own. Note this is not the 2014 Infinity Gauntlet Omnibus: that one is the event edition, with the Hulk, Doctor Strange and Quasar tie-ins and no annuals.
volumes.lede: Starlin turns the Surfer's own book into the launchpad for the biggest story Marvel has — which is both its achievement and its cost.
volumes.verdict: The Infinity Gauntlet is one of the most consequential Marvel stories ever published — it defined the cosmic corner of the universe for thirty years and supplied the plot of two of the highest-grossing films ever made.

volumes.title: Silver Surfer by Slott & Allred Omnibus
volumes.creators: Dan Slott & Michael Allred
volumes.note: Doctor Who with a surfboard, and it works. Dawn Greenwood gets in the way of the most humourless character Marvel has and Allred draws the result in pop primaries. Both series here, #1–15 and #1–14, plus the Point One prologue. Mind the jump: Silver Surfer (1987) #67–146, the 2003 Straczynski series and the 2011 mini sit in front of this book and none of them has an omnibus. The book before this one closes the first third of that hole.
volumes.lede: Doctor Who with a surfboard, in flat pop-art colour — and an Eisner-winning issue that has to be physically turned upside down.
volumes.verdict: Critically the best-received Silver Surfer run there has been, with an Eisner for its best-known issue and a conclusion readers frequently describe as genuinely affecting.

tone_modes.label: Most propaganda
tone_modes.description: 1941. Anthology issues, breakneck pacing, and a hero created to argue for a war America had not joined. Historically extraordinary, crude as comics.

tone_modes.label: Most Kirby
tone_modes.description: Two separate stretches, twelve years apart — the Tales of Suspense fight scenes, and the 1976 return with the Madbomb. Enormous, bombastic, unlike anyone else.

tone_modes.label: Most political
tone_modes.description: Englehart's Secret Empire, written during Watergate, where the trail leads to the White House and Steve Rogers quits over it.

tone_modes.label: Most human
tone_modes.description: Stern and Byrne giving him an apartment and a job, and #250 — the issue where he is offered the presidency and declines.

tone_modes.label: Best long haul
tone_modes.description: Ten years of Gruenwald, and the storyline where the government takes the identity away and gives it to somebody sincere and wrong.

tone_modes.label: Most spy novel
tone_modes.description: Brubaker. Cold War espionage with a war story under it, almost no superheroics, and the best-executed resurrection in Marvel's history.

tone_modes.label: Saddest
tone_modes.description: Eighteen issues after the title character is shot, about everyone he left. Widely considered the best thing Marvel published that year.

tone_modes.label: Strangest
tone_modes.description: Remender's Dimension Z — a year in an alien wasteland raising a child, modelled on Kirby rather than on anything modern.

tone_modes.label: Most argued about
tone_modes.description: Secret Empire. Cap as a lifelong Hydra agent who wins. Read it as an argument about complicity rather than as a twist.

tone_modes.label: Most thoughtful
tone_modes.description: Coates, asking what the symbol is worth after it has been disgraced, with a Red Skull who fights with words.

tone_modes.label: Kindest
tone_modes.description: Waid and Samnee's ten issues of a man driving across America being decent to people. Exactly what was needed and hard to find anywhere else.

volumes.title: Golden Age Captain America Omnibus
volumes.creators: Joe Simon & Jack Kirby
volumes.note: Where he starts: Simon and Kirby, twelve anthology issues, and a cover of Cap punching Hitler that ran a year before America entered the war. Each issue is a full book rather than a single story, so this is 12 issues and a great deal of comics.
volumes.lede: Simon and Kirby, twelve anthology issues, and a cover that punched Hitler nine months before America entered the war.
volumes.verdict: Treated as an artefact first and a reading experience second, and nobody pretends otherwise. The consensus is that the Kirby layouts are genuinely thrilling and the writing is what 1941 anthology comics were.

volumes.title: Golden Age Captain America Omnibus
volumes.creators: Stan Lee, Al Avison & Syd Shores
volumes.note: Simon and Kirby leave after #10 and the book carries on without them — this is #13–24, the stretch where a nineteen-year-old Stan Lee is writing some of it. The Golden Age run goes to #75 and the omnibus line stops here, so everything after 1943 is uncollected in this format.
volumes.lede: Simon and Kirby leave after #10 and the book carries on without them — with a nineteen-year-old Stan Lee writing some of it.
volumes.verdict: Rated below Vol. 1 for the obvious reason: the thing that made Vol. 1 extraordinary has left the building. The art is a capable imitation of Kirby and reads as one.

volumes.title: Captain America Omnibus
volumes.creators: Stan Lee & Jack Kirby
volumes.note: The thaw. Tales of Suspense #59–99 is Cap sharing a book with Iron Man ten pages at a time, and it is where Kirby works out what a Captain America fight scene looks like; then the split, and Captain America #100 onward as his own title again. The Red Skull, the Cosmic Cube, and Bucky's death told properly for the first time.
volumes.lede: The thaw. Five years of ten-page chapters in Tales of Suspense where Kirby invents the modern Captain America fight scene, then the title back at #100.
volumes.verdict: Very well regarded, with the caveat that the Tales of Suspense chapters are repetitive read in bulk — ten pages of fighting, monthly, for years. Most readers recommend dipping rather than marathoning.

volumes.title: Captain America Omnibus
volumes.creators: Stan Lee, Gene Colan & John Romita Sr.
volumes.note: #114–148, and the book stops being a war comic. Cap and the Falcon become a partnership and the title changes to say so; Colan draws New York like a crime film, and the stories start being about whether the man out of time has anything to say about 1971.
volumes.lede: The book stops being a war comic. Gene Colan draws New York like a crime film, and the title changes to say the Falcon is a partner.
volumes.verdict: Sits between two much-discussed volumes and gets less attention than it deserves. Readers who work through the shelf in order routinely report this as the surprise: the book grows up here, and the Falcon partnership is written with real warmth.

volumes.title: Captain America Omnibus
volumes.creators: Steve Englehart, Sal Buscema & Frank Robbins
volumes.note: #149–192, which is mostly Englehart, and contains the single most famous thing anyone has done with the character: the Secret Empire story, where the trail of a government conspiracy leads to the White House and Steve Rogers quits being Captain America over it. Published while Watergate was on television.
volumes.lede: Englehart's Secret Empire — the trail leads to the White House, and Steve Rogers quits. Published while Watergate was on television.
volumes.verdict: Very widely named the defining Captain America story, and the one most often cited when people argue the character is inherently political rather than inherently patriotic.

volumes.title: Captain America Omnibus
volumes.creators: Jack Kirby
volumes.note: Kirby comes back to the character he made and writes as well as draws him — #193–214, the Madbomb, the Swine, Arnim Zola, and the Bicentennial Battles treasury. Note this supersedes the separate Captain America by Jack Kirby Omnibus, which holds the same issues minus FOOM #11.
volumes.lede: Kirby comes back to the character he made and writes as well as draws him. The strangest and most argued-about volume on the shelf.
volumes.verdict: One of the most polarised books on this site. Its admirers call it uncut Kirby imagination and treat it as a late-career high point; its detractors find the plotting incoherent and the dialogue impenetrable, and point out that it discards the character work of the run before it.

volumes.title: Captain America Omnibus
volumes.creators: Roger Stern, John Byrne & Roger McKenzie
volumes.note: #215–260. The run people mean when they say Stern and Byrne only lasted nine issues but fixed the character — they give him an apartment, a job and a reason to be Steve Rogers, and the book keeps that shape after they leave.
volumes.lede: Stern and Byrne get nine issues and answer the question the book had avoided for forty years: who is Steve Rogers when he takes the costume off?
volumes.verdict: The Stern/Byrne issues have a reputation far larger than nine issues normally earn, and it is deserved: this is where the modern Steve Rogers is invented, and #250 is on most best-of lists.

volumes.title: Captain America by Mark Gruenwald Omnibus
volumes.creators: Mark Gruenwald, Paul Neary & Kieron Dwyer
volumes.note: Ten years on the book, which is still the longest anyone has managed. This is #307–350: the Scourge of the Underworld, Diamondback, and the Captain — the year the government takes the identity off Steve and gives it to John Walker, which is the story every screen version has borrowed since.
volumes.lede: The start of a decade on the book, and the storyline every screen version has borrowed since: the government takes the identity away.
volumes.verdict: The Captain is very widely considered one of the best Captain America stories ever told and the single most influential on later adaptations. Walker in particular is praised as a genuinely difficult character rather than a straw man.

volumes.title: Captain America by Mark Gruenwald Omnibus
volumes.creators: Mark Gruenwald, Kieron Dwyer & Ron Lim
volumes.note: #351–386, plus the Adventures of Captain America retelling of the origin. The Red Skull is back with a body he did not have before, Crossbones arrives, and Bloodstone hunts through a book that has settled into being a very well-made superhero comic every month.
volumes.lede: The middle of the decade: the Red Skull with a new body, Crossbones, and a book that has settled into being extremely good at its job.
volumes.verdict: Well liked without generating much argument. The recurring assessment is reliable, dense, workmanlike superhero comics by someone who understood the character better than almost anyone.

volumes.title: Captain America by Mark Gruenwald Omnibus
volumes.creators: Mark Gruenwald, Rik Levins & Dave Hoover
volumes.note: #387–418, Blood and Glory with the Punisher, and U.S.Agent's own mini. Operation: Galactic Storm runs through the middle of it. The run goes on to #443 and the omnibus line stops at #418, so the last two years of Gruenwald — Fighting Chance, and Cap's body failing him — are not collected here.
volumes.lede: The last collected stretch of the ten-year run, and the point at which the 1990s start pulling the book around.
volumes.verdict: Rated below the first two volumes, and the reasons given are mostly external: crossover interference, a house art style readers find less appealing than Dwyer's or Neary's, and the sense of a long run running down.

volumes.title: Captain America by Waid, Garney & Kubert Omnibus
volumes.creators: Mark Waid, Ron Garney & Andy Kubert
volumes.note: Two runs with Heroes Reborn in the gap between them. Waid and Garney take #444–454 and immediately bring Sharon Carter back from the dead; then the book is cancelled for the Heroes Reborn year, and they return for Captain America (1998) #1–23 plus the Sentinel of Liberty mini. The Heroes Reborn year itself is a different book and is not here.
chapters: Captain America: Sentinel of Liberty Rough Cut #1
volumes.lede: Two runs with a cancellation in the middle. Waid brings Sharon Carter back, Marvel cancels the book for Heroes Reborn, and then he comes back and relaunches it.
volumes.verdict: Regularly named the best Captain America between Gruenwald and Brubaker, and singled out for treating sincerity as a strength at a moment when the industry was doing the opposite.

volumes.title: Captain America by Dan Jurgens Omnibus
volumes.creators: Dan Jurgens & Andy Kubert
volumes.note: Captain America (1998) #25–50, which finishes that volume. Jurgens writes and draws most of it — Protocide, the Red Skull's return, and a Korea story that is the book at its best. After this the title relaunches twice more before anything is collected again.
volumes.lede: The end of the 1998 volume, written and drawn largely by one person, with a Korea story that is the best thing in it.
volumes.verdict: Barely discussed, and the readers who have read it tend to describe it as better than its invisibility suggests — well-constructed, traditional superhero comics from someone who clearly likes the character.

volumes.title: Captain America by Ed Brubaker Omnibus
volumes.creators: Ed Brubaker, Steve Epting & Michael Lark
volumes.note: Captain America (2004) #1–25, and the run that reset the character for twenty years. Brubaker writes it as a spy thriller, Epting draws it like one, and the thing everyone said could not be done — bringing Bucky back — turns out to be the best idea anyone had had about Cap in decades.
volumes.lede: The run that reset the character for twenty years, by changing genre and by doing the one thing everybody said could not be done.
volumes.verdict: Almost universally named the best modern Captain America run and one of the best Marvel runs of the century. The Winter Soldier is treated as a rare genuinely great addition to a sixty-year-old mythology, and the MCU took it almost wholesale.

volumes.title: Death of Captain America Omnibus
volumes.creators: Ed Brubaker & Steve Epting
volumes.note: #25–42, straight on from the Brubaker volume, which is why #25 is in both books. Steve is shot on the courthouse steps and the book keeps going for eighteen issues about everyone else — Bucky, Sharon, the Falcon, the Red Skull — which is the trick of it: the title character is dead and it is still the best comic Marvel is publishing.
volumes.lede: He is shot on the courthouse steps in the first issue, and the book runs for eighteen more about everyone else. It is the best thing Marvel published that year.
volumes.verdict: Frequently rated even higher than the run that precedes it, on the grounds that sustaining a title for eighteen issues without its lead is a genuinely hard thing to do and this does it without strain.

volumes.title: Captain America Lives! Omnibus
volumes.creators: Ed Brubaker, Butch Guice & Bryan Hitch
volumes.note: #43–601 and the Reborn mini — how they undid it. Bucky is wearing the costume and carrying a gun, which the book takes seriously as a problem, and Steve is unstuck in his own timeline rather than simply dead. Note the numbering jumps to #600 partway through: the title reverted to its original count for the anniversary.
volumes.lede: How they undid it, and the eighteen months of Bucky carrying the shield first.
volumes.verdict: Solidly liked, and rated below the two volumes before it for a structural reason rather than a quality one: it is the book that has to undo the best story, and everyone knew it was coming.

volumes.title: Captain America: The Trial of Captain America Omnibus
volumes.creators: Ed Brubaker, Butch Guice & Mitch Breitweiser
volumes.note: #602–619 and then Captain America (2011) #1–10, with Steve Rogers: Super-Soldier alongside. Bucky is put on trial for what he did as the Winter Soldier, which is the question the whole Brubaker run has been circling: whether a man is guilty of things done while he was someone else's weapon.
chapters: Captain America: Who Will Wield  the Shield? #1
volumes.lede: Bucky is put on trial for what he did as the Winter Soldier — which is the question the whole Brubaker run has been circling.
