volumes.verdict: Well received and somewhat overshadowed by the more famous volumes around it. Readers who rate it highly point at the moral seriousness — it is the payoff to five years of setup and it does not flinch.

volumes.title: Captain America: Return of the Winter Soldier Omnibus
volumes.creators: Ed Brubaker, Butch Guice & Chris Samnee
volumes.note: The end of Brubaker's eight years. Captain America and Bucky, the Fear Itself tie-ins, Captain America (2011) #11–19, and the whole Winter Soldier ongoing — fourteen issues of Bucky running black operations that Cap is not told about, which is the closest this run comes to a spy book with no superheroes in it at all.
volumes.lede: The end of Brubaker's eight years, including fourteen issues of Bucky running black operations Cap is not told about.
volumes.verdict: The Winter Soldier ongoing is the part people praise, and it is often recommended on its own to readers who like espionage fiction and do not care about superheroes at all.

volumes.title: Captain America by Rick Remender Omnibus
volumes.creators: Rick Remender, John Romita Jr. & Carlos Pacheco
volumes.note: Captain America (2012) #1–25 and then All-New Captain America. Remender opens by stranding Steve in Dimension Z for a year of publishing, raising a child there, which is either the boldest thing anyone has done with the book or a very long detour depending on who you ask. It ends with the serum gone and Sam Wilson carrying the shield.
volumes.lede: Follow the best modern run by doing the opposite: strand him in an alien dimension for a year and make him raise a child there.
volumes.verdict: Genuinely split. Admirers call it brave and ambitious and the only modern run with the nerve to be strange; detractors call Dimension Z an enormous detour that removed Captain America from Captain America's book for a year.

volumes.title: Captain America by Nick Spencer Omnibus
volumes.creators: Nick Spencer, Daniel Acuña & Jesus Saiz
volumes.note: Two Captains at once: Sam Wilson has the shield and a book about how much of America hates him for what he says with it, and Steve Rogers gets his youth back and a secret. Standoff runs through the middle. This is the setup for the thing everyone remembers, and it is better read as the argument it actually is than as the twist.
chapters: Avengers Standoff: Welcome to Pleasant Hill #1
Avengers Standoff: Assault on Pleasant Hill Alpha #1
Avengers Standoff: Assault on Pleasant Hill Omega #1
volumes.lede: Two Captains at once: Sam Wilson holding the shield and being hated for what he says with it, and Steve Rogers restored to youth with a secret.
volumes.verdict: Overshadowed entirely by what it sets up, which is a shame: the Sam Wilson material is very well regarded by the readers who got to it, and is frequently described as the most substantial political writing the book has had in decades.

volumes.title: Captain America by Nick Spencer Omnibus
volumes.creators: Nick Spencer, Andrea Sorrentino & Daniel Acuña
volumes.note: Secret Empire, and the rest of both books around it. Cap has been a Hydra sleeper the whole time and wins; the story is about what the country does while he does it. Divisive on publication and still is. Ends with Generations and the restoration.
chapters: Generations: Sam Wilson Captain America & Steve Rogers Captain America #1
volumes.lede: Secret Empire. Captain America has been a Hydra sleeper his whole life, and he wins. The most controversial Marvel story of its decade.
volumes.verdict: The most contested book on this shelf. Reviews at the time were mixed, and the discourse around it was substantially larger and angrier than the reviews.

volumes.title: Black Widow & Captain America by Waid & Samnee Omnibus
volumes.creators: Mark Waid & Chris Samnee
volumes.note: Half of this is Black Widow's book, and it is on the shelf anyway because the other half — Captain America (2017) #695–704 — is collected in omnibus nowhere else. Waid and Samnee put Steve back in the costume after Secret Empire and write ten issues of deliberately uncomplicated Captain America, which after the previous volume is the point.
volumes.lede: Half of this is Black Widow's book. It is on the shelf because the other half — ten issues of deliberately uncomplicated Captain America — is collected nowhere else.
volumes.verdict: The Captain America half is warmly received as exactly the right book at exactly the right moment, and Samnee's art gets consistent praise.

volumes.title: Captain America by Ta-Nehisi Coates Omnibus
volumes.creators: Ta-Nehisi Coates, Leinil Francis Yu & Adam Kubert
volumes.note: Captain America (2018) #1–30, the whole run. Coates writes a Steve Rogers who has come out of Secret Empire with his reputation wrecked and no idea what the symbol is worth any more, and answers it slowly, through the Power Elite and a Red Skull who fights with rhetoric rather than a gun.
volumes.lede: The whole run: a Steve Rogers whose reputation has been destroyed, asking slowly whether the symbol is worth anything any more.
volumes.verdict: The recurring phrase in reviews is almost exactly that: uneven but always thoughtful. The ideas and the internal narration get consistent praise, and the conclusion in #30 was well received as a fitting end.

tone_modes.label: Most Cold War
tone_modes.description: The Tales of Suspense years: communist villains, military hardware, and a book entirely comfortable with the arms trade. A period document.

tone_modes.label: Most Bronze Age
tone_modes.description: Goodwin and Tuska through the 70s — blunt, solid superhero comics, and the issue where Thanos turns up.

tone_modes.label: Most human
tone_modes.description: Demon in a Bottle. Alcoholism written as a condition rather than a lesson, over months, with real damage. The run that made the character serious.

tone_modes.label: Best premise
tone_modes.description: Armor Wars — the hero as the problem, hunting his own technology through other people's suits and becoming a fugitive for it.

tone_modes.label: Most traditional
tone_modes.description: Busiek and Chen rebuilding the book after Heroes Reborn. Unfashionable, well-made, and a good place to start.

tone_modes.label: Strangest
tone_modes.description: The armour develops an intelligence, falls in love with Tony, and tries to replace him. Body horror in a Marvel monthly.

tone_modes.label: Funniest and most modern
tone_modes.description: Slott on simulation, copies and digital minds — the character's actual 21st-century problem, played for ideas and jokes.

volumes.title: Invincible Iron Man Omnibus
volumes.creators: Stan Lee, Don Heck & Gene Colan
volumes.note: A weapons manufacturer is wounded by his own landmine, builds a suit of armour to keep his heart beating, and spends the next sixty years failing to put it down. Tales of Suspense #39 is the origin; the grey armour is gold by #40 and red-and-gold by #48, which is Marvel deciding what the character looks like in real time. Heck, Ditko and then Colan draw it, the Mandarin and the Crimson Dynamo turn up, and the Tales to Astonish at the end is the Sub-Mariner crossover.
volumes.lede: The debut, the grey armour, and the redesign that made him legible. A Cold War comic with a life-support machine at the centre of it.
volumes.verdict: Rated below the equivalent Spider-Man and Fantastic Four volumes by most readers, and the reasons given are consistent: the ten-page format is restrictive, the villains are interchangeable communists, and the politics are very much of 1963.

volumes.title: Invincible Iron Man Omnibus
volumes.creators: Stan Lee, Archie Goodwin & Gene Colan
volumes.note: The back half of Tales of Suspense, then his own title at last. Iron Man and Sub-Mariner #1 is the hinge — a one-shot in April 1968 that exists purely because the shared book was splitting in two, and it sits here between Tales of Suspense #99 and Iron Man #1, which is where it was published and where it reads. Archie Goodwin takes over and brings Madame Masque and Whiplash with him.
volumes.lede: The end of the shared book and the start of the solo one, with Archie Goodwin arriving to give the character something to be about.
volumes.verdict: Better received than Vol. 1, and the reason is Goodwin — readers consistently name his issues as the point where the series starts having ideas rather than just villains.

volumes.title: Invincible Iron Man Omnibus
volumes.creators: Archie Goodwin, Gerry Conway & George Tuska
volumes.note: Fourteen years after the volume before it, which is Marvel finally finishing a numbered run. Goodwin closes out, Conway and Tuska take over, and Iron Man #55 quietly introduces Thanos, Drax and Moondragon in a single issue — the most consequential twenty pages on this shelf by some distance. The Daredevil at the end is the other half of a crossover.
volumes.lede: The Bronze Age arrives, the arms trade stops being neutral, and Thanos turns up in the middle of an ordinary issue.
volumes.verdict: Its reputation is dominated by #55, and the rest is a solid, unglamorous Bronze Age run that readers working through the shelf report enjoying more than they expected.

volumes.title: Invincible Iron Man Omnibus
volumes.creators: Mike Friedrich, Bill Mantlo & George Tuska
volumes.note: The stretch nobody quotes and most people have not read. Friedrich and then Bill Mantlo run the book for four years, rebuild the armour, bring back Madame Masque and thread Jack of Hearts through the drama; there are team-ups with Daredevil, Man-Thing and the Champions. It stops at #112, and Mantlo's #113–114 are collected nowhere at all — a two-issue hole before the next book opens at #115.
volumes.lede: The last of the numbered volumes: Mantlo and Friedrich, #100, and the run-up to the book's best decade.
volumes.verdict: The least-discussed of the four numbered volumes and rated accordingly: well-made 1970s superhero comics with no landmark in them beyond #100.

volumes.title: Iron Man by Michelinie, Layton & Romita Jr. Omnibus
volumes.creators: David Michelinie, Bob Layton & John Romita Jr.
volumes.note: The run that made Tony Stark a character rather than a suit. "Demon in a Bottle" is nine issues of him drinking himself out of his own company, and it is still the thing every later writer is answering; Doomquest drops him and Doctor Doom into Arthurian Britain, Justin Hammer arrives, and the space and stealth armours get built. Forty-three issues with no filler in them.
volumes.lede: The run that made Iron Man serious. Demon in a Bottle, Doomquest, and an inker who made the armour look like metal.
volumes.verdict: Very widely named the definitive Iron Man run, and Demon in a Bottle is on essentially every best-Marvel-story list ever compiled. Its influence on later Iron Man — including the films — is enormous.

volumes.title: Iron Man: Armor Wars Omnibus
volumes.creators: David Michelinie, Bob Layton & Mark Bright
volumes.note: Michelinie and Layton come back for the story with the best premise in the character: his technology has been stolen, it is inside half the armoured villains in the Marvel Universe, and he decides to go and take it back whether or not anyone has asked him to. Armor Wars is #219–232 and the sequel is #258–266; the twenty-five issues between them are not here because this is a storyline book, not a run. Mind the jump to get to it — #158–218 has never been collected in omnibus.
volumes.lede: The best premise anyone has built for this character: his technology is in other people's hands and he decides to take it back, whatever that costs.
volumes.verdict: The original Armor Wars is very highly rated and is the Iron Man story most often named alongside Demon in a Bottle. Its central idea — the hero as the antagonist of his own story — is the one that has aged best.

volumes.title: Iron Man by Kurt Busiek & Sean Chen Omnibus
volumes.creators: Kurt Busiek & Sean Chen
volumes.note: Heroes Return: the third Iron Man #1, and Busiek writing him as a man who is good at engineering and bad at everything else. The nine single issues after the run are "The Eighth Day" crossover, one chapter per book, and The Iron Age closes it. There is a long way to fall to get here — Iron Man #267–332 and the whole Heroes Reborn year sit in front of this book and none of it has an omnibus.
volumes.lede: The relaunch after Heroes Reborn. Traditional, well-made, and deliberately unfashionable — and the best place on this shelf to start cold.
volumes.verdict: Under-discussed and warmly regarded by the people who have read it. The recurring assessment is solid, generous, traditional superhero comics by a writer who understood exactly what the book needed after four chaotic years.

volumes.title: Iron Man: The Mask in the Iron Man Omnibus
volumes.creators: Joe Quesada, Frank Tieri & Sean Chen
volumes.note: Quesada's answer to "what if the armour woke up": it becomes sentient, it is in love with him, and it is not going to take being switched off well. Tieri runs the back half into Sons of Yinsen. It picks up directly where the Busiek book stops, at #26, and runs to the end of the volume at #49 with both annuals and the Wizard mail-away half-issue.
volumes.lede: The armour develops an artificial intelligence, falls in love with Tony, and decides the world would be better without him. Easily the strangest book on this shelf.
volumes.verdict: The reception is unusually consistent and unusually shaped: readers love the opening arc and report the run getting steadily worse from there. The phrase that recurs is that it is worth reading for the first story.

volumes.title: Tony Stark: Iron Man by Dan Slott Omnibus
volumes.creators: Dan Slott, Jim Zub & Valerio Schiti
volumes.note: Slott builds the eScape, a virtual world nobody can prove they have left, and then asks Tony to work out whether he is a man or a very good copy of one. Iron Man 2020 hands the book to Arno Stark and a robot uprising. The Busiek issue printed at the back is not a mistake: Iron Man (1998) #25 is where Arno was set up, twenty years earlier, and the book reprints it so the ending lands. Another long jump to get here — everything between 2002 and 2018 is uncollected in omnibus.
volumes.lede: The most modern book here: simulation, digital minds, and whether a backed-up copy of a person is that person. Also the funniest.
volumes.verdict: Received as a smart, funny, conceptually ambitious run that gets less attention than it deserves, largely because it followed a long period of the character being difficult to publish.

tone_modes.label: Most important
tone_modes.description: McGregor's Jungle Action, inside the first volume — thirteen issues of one story in 1973, an all-Black cast, and Killmonger. If you read one thing here for its place in history, this.

tone_modes.label: Best written
tone_modes.description: Priest, across two volumes. A geopolitical thriller told backwards by a panicking bureaucrat, and the consensus best run the character has had.

tone_modes.label: Purest Kirby
tone_modes.description: The 1977 solo run, in Panther's Prey. Time-travelling frogs, an immortal samurai, no continuity and no apologies. Kirby at seventy.

tone_modes.label: Closest to the films
tone_modes.description: Hudlin. The origin restaged as a war movie by Romita Jr., Shuri made central, and Wakanda written as a superpower.

tone_modes.label: Most ambitious
tone_modes.description: Coates. Fifty issues on whether a hereditary monarch can be a hero, half of it as an anti-imperial space epic, and the suit redesign everyone now uses.

tone_modes.label: Bleakest
tone_modes.description: “Panther's Quest”, inside Panther's Prey — twenty-five eight-page chapters in apartheid South Africa, with every advantage taken off him. Colan drawing at his loosest.

tone_modes.label: Everybody else's Wakanda
tone_modes.description: The anthology — Roxane Gay on the Dora Milaje, Nnedi Okorafor on Shuri, Bryan Hill on Killmonger. A third of it is not about T'Challa at all.

volumes.title: Black Panther: The Early Marvel Years Omnibus
volumes.creators: Stan Lee, Jack Kirby, Roy Thomas & Don McGregor
volumes.note: Ten years of being the best character in other people's comics, and then his own. Fantastic Four #52 is the first Black superhero in mainstream American comics and Kirby draws him as a head of state rather than a jungle lord; the Avengers issues are Roy Thomas working out what T'Challa is when he is not a guest. Then the last third of the book is Don McGregor's Jungle Action — “Panther's Rage”, thirteen issues of one continuous story at a time when nobody serialised anything, with Rich Buckler and Billy Graham on it and a page density that still reads as unusual.
volumes.lede: Ten years as the best character in other people's comics, and then the thirteen-issue story that changed what a superhero comic could be.
volumes.standing: Landmark, and half of it is guest appearances
volumes.verdict: “Panther's Rage” has no serious detractors. Its reputation grew enormously after the 2018 film and it is now the piece of Black Panther comics most often named by people outside comics, usually for the same two reasons: the thirteen-issue structure and Killmonger.

volumes.title: Black Panther: Panther's Prey Omnibus
volumes.creators: Jack Kirby, Peter B. Gillis & Don McGregor
volumes.note: The messy two decades, and the most interesting book on the shelf for it. Kirby comes back for fifteen issues and writes an outright pulp adventure — King Solomon's Frogs, time travel, a six-armed collector — which readers of Jungle Action hated and which is now the reason people buy this. Then the 1988 Gillis mini, Don McGregor and Dwayne Turner's Panther's Prey in 1991, and twenty-five chapters of Panther's Quest serialised eight pages at a time in Marvel Comics Presents. Solicited as “Revenge of the Black Panther” and retitled before it shipped.
volumes.lede: Kirby's own pulp run, then two decades of the character having nowhere to live — including the bleakest story anybody has told about him.
volumes.verdict: This is the volume with the widest spread of opinion on it, because it is three different books. Kirby's run is now well liked and was not at the time; “Panther's Quest” is admired and rarely reread, because it is genuinely punishing; and the tail is guest spots and oddities.

volumes.title: Black Panther by Christopher Priest Omnibus
volumes.creators: Christopher Priest, Mark Texeira & Sal Velluto
volumes.note: The run that decided what the character is now. Priest tells it out of order through Everett K. Ross, a State Department attaché narrating a disaster from a chair, and the joke covers a straight political thriller about a head of state who joined the Avengers to spy on them. The Dora Milaje are invented here. So is the idea that T'Challa is always three moves ahead, which every later writer and both films inherited.
volumes.lede: The run that decided what the character is. A political thriller told out of order by a State Department attaché who is not coping.
volumes.verdict: This is as close to a settled verdict as this shelf has. Priest's run is routinely named among the best superhero runs of its era, is the run creators cite when asked about the character, and its inventions — Ross, the Dora Milaje, the always-three-moves-ahead T'Challa — went into the films essentially intact.

volumes.title: Black Panther by Christopher Priest Omnibus
volumes.creators: Christopher Priest, Sal Velluto & Jim Calafiore
volumes.note: The back half of the run, where it goes strange: the Sturm und Drang of the Iron Man fight, the King Solomon's Frogs paying off in a second Panther out of the future, and then Marvel takes the title off T'Challa entirely and hands it to Kevin “Kasper” Cole, a crooked Harlem cop in a stolen costume. That becomes The Crew, cancelled at seven issues and quietly one of the best things Priest wrote. The 1986 date on this tile is Thor #370 — an eight-page Black Panther backup by James Owsley, which is Priest under his own earlier name and the first Panther story he ever wrote.
volumes.lede: The back half, where the run gets stranger, loses its lead character on purpose, and ends on a cancelled masterpiece.
volumes.standing: Great, and it commits commercial suicide
volumes.verdict: Readers who love the first volume mostly love this one too, and The Crew in particular has a devoted following well out of proportion to its seven issues — Priest has said it is among his favourite work, and its cancellation is a standing grievance.

volumes.title: Black Panther by Reginald Hudlin Omnibus
volumes.creators: Reginald Hudlin, John Romita Jr. & Ken Lashley
volumes.note: A film-maker's Black Panther, and the one the MCU actually drew on. Hudlin restarts from the origin with Romita Jr. drawing Wakanda as a superpower that has never lost a war, marries T'Challa to Storm across a company-wide crossover, sends the two of them through Civil War and Secret Invasion, and then puts Shuri in the suit for the 2009 series — which is where nearly everything the films did with her comes from. The X-Men issues are printed in crossover order rather than after the run, which is how the book prints them.
chapters: Captain America/Black Panther: Flags of Our Fathers #1–4
volumes.lede: A film director's Black Panther — the origin restaged at blockbuster scale, a royal wedding, and Shuri in the suit nine years before the film.
volumes.standing: The most divisive book on the shelf
volumes.verdict: The defence is straightforward and mostly holds: it is the most confident and most accessible Black Panther has ever been, Romita Jr.'s opening arc looks superb, and it is the run the 2018 film borrowed most structurally — Shuri's whole screen presence starts here.

volumes.title: Black Panther by Ta-Nehisi Coates Omnibus
volumes.creators: Ta-Nehisi Coates, Brian Stelfreeze & Daniel Acuña
volumes.note: An essayist's Black Panther: fifty issues asking whether a hereditary monarch can be a hero at all, and mostly answering no. Stelfreeze's first arc is a Wakandan insurrection T'Challa cannot punch, and the second half moves the whole argument into space as the Intergalactic Empire of Wakanda — a slave state flying his own flag, five thousand years old, which he has to bring down without a memory of who he is. The longest single Black Panther run there has been.
volumes.lede: Fifty issues on whether a hereditary king can be a hero, half of them as an anti-imperial space epic. The longest run the character has had.
volumes.verdict: The praise is for scope. This is the most politically serious Black Panther has been, the Stelfreeze design is now the definitive one, and the premise of the second half — the hero's own country as the empire — is genuinely bold for a licensed superhero book.

volumes.title: Wakanda: World of Black Panther Omnibus
volumes.creators: Nnedi Okorafor, Roxane Gay & Evan Narcisse
volumes.note: Everything that grew up around the Coates run — the country as a setting other writers were let into. Roxane Gay and Yona Harvey on the Dora Milaje in World of Wakanda, Nnedi Okorafor on Shuri and on Long Live the King, Bryan Hill on Killmonger's making, Evan Narcisse retelling the origin in Rise of the Black Panther, and the Wakanda Forever one-shots. Note this is the one book on the shelf that is not a Black Panther title: about a third of it stars somebody else, and it doubles back over the Coates and Hudlin volumes for four issues.
chapters: Black Panther: Long Live the King #1–6
Black Panther and the Agents of Wakanda #1–8
volumes.lede: The country as a setting other people were let into — the Dora Milaje, Shuri, Killmonger. About a third of it is not about T'Challa at all.
volumes.standing: An anthology, with the range that implies
volumes.verdict: Judge it by the parts, because it is not a run. Shuri and World of Wakanda are both well regarded, and The Crew's cancellation after two issues on sale is a standing complaint — several of the best things here were killed before they finished.

tone_modes.label: Most 1990s
tone_modes.description: The three Danny Ketch volumes, and Vol. 2 especially. Texeira's black ink, an entire horror imprint launched off one title's sales, and a seventeen-part crossover. Start here if you want the version that sold.

tone_modes.label: Most horror
tone_modes.description: Percy's run. A small town that is wrong, dread built on a schedule, and a novelist's pacing. The only book here that is frightening rather than loud.

tone_modes.label: Most ambitious
tone_modes.description: Jason Aaron. Reassigns the curse from hell to heaven, invents a lineage of Riders going back centuries, and actually finishes what it started.

tone_modes.label: Strangest
tone_modes.description: Ghost Rider 2099. Straight-faced cyberpunk with a warbot in the lead, written five years before The Matrix and drawn by early Chris Bachalo. A different man, a different genre, complete in 25 issues.

tone_modes.label: Funniest
tone_modes.description: Cosmic Ghost Rider. The Punisher a thousand years on, doing bits. No curse, no penance, no haunting — and two-thirds of the volume is other people's comics.

volumes.title: Ghost Rider: Danny Ketch Omnibus
volumes.creators: Howard Mackie, Javier Saltares & Mark Texeira
volumes.note: Marvel's best-selling book of 1990, and the shelf starts here because Johnny Blaze's 1972 run has never been collected in omnibus at all. Danny Ketch finds a motorcycle in a scrapyard, touches its gas cap and burns. Howard Mackie writes him as a teenager who cannot control the thing wearing him — the Rider does the talking, decides who is guilty and is not remotely on Danny's side. Javier Saltares lays it out and then Mark Texeira inks over him from #6 and the book turns into scratched black ink and hellfire, which is the look the whole decade copied. The Hearts of Darkness one-shot with Wolverine and the Punisher is in here, and so is fifty-five issues' worth of Marvel Comics Presents backups.
volumes.lede: A new man in the head, the Penance Stare, and Mark Texeira inventing the way the whole decade would look.
volumes.verdict: This is the version of Ghost Rider that sold in enormous numbers, and the affection for it is real and largely nostalgic — readers who were fourteen in 1990 rate it very highly indeed.

volumes.title: Ghost Rider: Danny Ketch Omnibus
volumes.creators: Howard Mackie, Andy Kubert & Adam Kubert
volumes.note: Johnny Blaze comes back, the two of them get a second book — Spirits of Vengeance, with Adam Kubert drawing it — and then Marvel builds an entire horror line around them. Rise of the Midnight Sons runs through six titles at once and this volume prints all of it: Morbius, Nightstalkers, Darkhold and Doctor Strange alongside the two Ghost Rider titles, in the order the crossover was read. It is the most 1993 thing on the site and it is also the moment the character stopped being a solo book and became a franchise.
chapters: Darkhold: Pages from the Book of Sins #1
Darkhold: Pages from the Book of Sins #11
volumes.lede: Johnny Blaze comes back, the two Riders get a second title, and Marvel builds an entire horror imprint on the back of one hit.
volumes.verdict: The Midnight Sons era is the character's commercial high point and its critical low, and both are true at once. This is crossover-driven publishing at the height of the speculator boom, with all the padding that implies.

volumes.title: Ghost Rider: Danny Ketch Omnibus
volumes.creators: Howard Mackie, Ron Garney & Adam Kubert
volumes.note: Ships October 2026 — it is on the shelf ahead of that because its contents, its links and its jacket are all real, which is the bar a tile has to clear. Ron Garney takes over the pencils and the run peaks: Siege of Darkness closes the Midnight Sons story across every book at once, and Ghost Rider #50 is the double-length anniversary issue with five artists on it. The tail of the book is the strangest material on the shelf — Blaze: Legacy of Blood, and the single issue of Ghost Rider and the Midnight Sons Magazine, neither of which is on Marvel Unlimited.
chapters: Darkhold: Pages from the Book of Sins #15
Darkhold: Pages from the Book of Sins #16
Ghost Rider and the Midnight Sons Magazine #1
volumes.lede: Siege of Darkness, Ron Garney's arrival, and the double-length #50 — the last good year before the line collapsed.
volumes.standing: The best of the Mackie run
volumes.verdict: Readers who rate the 1990s Ghost Rider highly usually mean this stretch — Garney's art, the Blaze/Ketch double act at full strength, and a crossover with an actual ending.

volumes.title: Ghost Rider 2099 Omnibus
volumes.creators: Len Kaminski & Chris Bachalo
volumes.note: Zero Cochrane is shot to death by corporate security, has his mind uploaded to the net by three ghosts in the machine and comes back inside a cybernetic warbot. It is cyberpunk between Neuromancer and The Matrix, written by Len Kaminski with a straight face, and Chris Bachalo draws the first stretch of it — early Bachalo, all compressed panels and machinery. A different man under the name, on the shelf for the reason Maestro is on the Hulk shelf: every issue in it is a Ghost Rider book. All 25 issues, complete.
volumes.lede: A murdered hacker downloaded into a warbot. Straight-faced cyberpunk, complete in twenty-five issues, and drawn by Chris Bachalo before anyone knew who that was.
volumes.verdict: Nearly forgotten for twenty-five years and then increasingly well spoken of, for the usual cult reasons: it is short, it is complete, it commits to its premise, and it looks like nothing else with the name on it.

volumes.title: Ghost Rider by Jason Aaron Omnibus
volumes.creators: Jason Aaron, Roland Boschi & Tony Moore
volumes.note: Aaron's answer to the question nobody had asked: what if the thing that made Johnny Blaze a Ghost Rider was not the devil at all. Zadkiel is a rogue angel raiding heaven, the Riders turn out to be a lineage going back centuries, and the book becomes a road movie with a nun on a motorcycle and a caretaker with a shotgun. Note it opens at Ghost Rider (2006) #20 — Daniel Way wrote #1–19 and that stretch has no omnibus, so the volume starts where Aaron does. Ends on the Heaven's on Fire mini, which is the finale.
volumes.lede: The curse comes from heaven, not hell — and the book becomes a road movie with a nun, a shotgun and a war in the sky.
volumes.verdict: Widely held to be the best sustained run the character has had, and the one most often recommended to a reader who has never picked up a Ghost Rider comic. Aaron went on to Thor, Southern Bastards and a five-year Avengers run, and this is where a lot of people first noticed him.

volumes.title: Cosmic Ghost Rider Omnibus
volumes.creators: Donny Cates, Geoff Shaw & Dylan Burnett
volumes.note: Frank Castle made a deal with the devil, then a deal with Galactus, then a deal with Thanos, and turns up a thousand years in the future as a chain-swinging lunatic on a flaming space bike. He is a joke that Donny Cates keeps refusing to stop telling until it turns into something sad. The odd volume on this shelf and knowingly so: seventeen of its thirty-five issues are Thanos, Guardians of the Galaxy and Avengers comics rather than his own, because that is where the character was invented and where he kept turning up. Starts with the Thanos issues that created him.
chapters: Cosmic Ghost Rider Destroys Marvel History #1–6
Revenge of the Cosmic Ghost Rider #1–5
volumes.lede: Frank Castle, a thousand years dead, on a burning space bike — and two-thirds of this book is other people's comics.
volumes.standing: Very funny, barely a Ghost Rider book
volumes.verdict: Thanos Wins is the part everyone rates, and it is genuinely one of the best-regarded cosmic Marvel stories of the last decade. The Cosmic Ghost Rider material that follows is fondly held but is understood as a comedy spin-off, and the reception thins out across the later minis.

volumes.title: Ghost Rider by Benjamin Percy Omnibus
volumes.creators: Benjamin Percy & Cory Smith
volumes.note: Ships October 2026, on the shelf early for the same reason Vol. 3 is. Percy is a horror novelist and he writes it as one: Johnny Blaze wakes up in a small town with a wife and two children and a life he does not remember earning, and the book spends five issues letting you work out what that is. It runs from there through the Wolverine crossover into Final Vengeance, which is the last Ghost Rider story before the title went away — so this is currently the end of the shelf as well as the end of the run.
chapters: Ghost Rider/Wolverine: Weapons of Vengeance Alpha #1
Ghost Rider/Wolverine: Weapons of Vengeance Omega #1
volumes.lede: A horror novelist gets the fiftieth-anniversary relaunch and opens it with Johnny Blaze in a small town that does not exist.
volumes.verdict: Well received, and specifically praised for treating the book as horror rather than as an action title with a skull in it — which readers note is rarer than it should be for this character.

tone_modes.label: Strangest-looking
tone_modes.description: Ditko's five-page backups. Impossible architecture drawn flat and hard, and the moment the universe turns out to be a man-shaped hole full of stars.

tone_modes.label: Best-drawn
tone_modes.description: Englehart and Brunner, then Colan. Art Nouveau borders, deep blacks, and a story that goes back to the moment of creation and finds somebody already there.

tone_modes.label: Funniest, and then not
tone_modes.description: Gerber's Defenders. The Headmen, Bambi and the Bozos, and an elf who shoots a stranger for no reason anyone ever explains.

tone_modes.label: Most consequential team book
tone_modes.description: The non-team's first five years, including the Avengers/Defenders War — the first great hero-versus-hero crossover.

tone_modes.label: Most like a job
tone_modes.description: Sorcerer Supreme. Ninety issues of rules, costs, precedent and paperwork, with Roy Thomas treating sixty years of continuity as a case file.

tone_modes.label: Oddest
tone_modes.description: The end of Sorcerer Supreme — Strange loses his powers and starts drawing on the Vapors, a bargain readers have argued about for thirty years.

tone_modes.label: Best modern idea
tone_modes.description: Aaron and Bachalo. Magic has a price, Strange is in debt for all of it, and then someone burns magic out of the world.

tone_modes.label: Best plotted
tone_modes.description: MacKay. A murder mystery where the detective is the victim, and then ten issues of Clea being better at his job than he was.

volumes.title: Doctor Strange Omnibus
volumes.creators: Stan Lee & Steve Ditko
volumes.note: Five pages a month at the back of a Human Torch book, and it became the strangest thing Marvel published. Steve Ditko had nowhere to put a fight scene in that page count, so he drew rooms instead — folded staircases, floating rock, planes of colour with no horizon — and invented what a magic dimension looks like in comics. Stan Lee's captions name things rather than explain them, which is why the Vishanti and the Dread Dormammu sound like real oaths. The Eternity saga in #130–146 is the run everyone means: seventeen issues of a chase across realities that ends with Strange meeting the universe itself, drawn as a man-shaped hole full of stars. Starts at Strange Tales #110 — note the strip skipped #112–113, so the book does too.
volumes.lede: Thirty-five five-page backup strips that invented what magic looks like in comics, and one Spider-Man annual.
volumes.standing: The foundation, and still the strangest-looking
volumes.verdict: Widely held to be one of the two or three most influential visual runs of the Silver Age, and the reason the character exists in the form he does. The Eternity sequence in particular is reproduced constantly well outside comics.

volumes.title: Doctor Strange Omnibus
volumes.creators: Roy Thomas, Gene Colan & Marie Severin
volumes.note: Ditko walks, and the book has to work out what it is without him. Marie Severin and then Gene Colan take it somewhere softer and more fleshy — Colan draws Strange as a man with weight and worry, in smoke and half-light rather than Ditko's hard geometry. Roy Thomas gives him a mask and a costume for a while, which everyone remembers as a mistake and which is genuinely worth seeing. Strange Tales #168 is the last issue of that title and Doctor Strange #169 picks the numbering straight up, so the two halves of this book are one continuous run. It ends with the title cancelled at #183, three guest appearances keeping him alive, and Marvel Feature #1 — where he calls the Hulk and the Sub-Mariner and accidentally starts the Defenders.
volumes.lede: Ditko leaves, Colan arrives, the strip graduates to its own title, and it is cancelled inside two years.
volumes.standing: A transitional book, and the mask is genuinely divisive
volumes.verdict: Readers split on this era. The case for it is Colan, who is one of the great Marvel artists and who gives the character a physical presence Ditko never aimed for. The case against is that the writing drifts, chasing a superhero register that does not suit the strip — and the costume is the emblem of that.

volumes.title: Defenders Omnibus
volumes.creators: Roy Thomas, Steve Englehart & Sal Buscema
volumes.note: Picks up on the issue the last book ended on. The joke of the Defenders is that it is an Avengers comic where nobody likes each other and there is no mansion, no butler and no charter — Strange is the only one who wants the team to exist, and he spends five years talking the Hulk and the Sub-Mariner into things. Sal Buscema draws almost all of it and gives the book its plain, sturdy, unglamorous look, which is exactly right for a group this shabby. The Avengers/Defenders War is here, the first great hero-versus-hero crossover and still one of the best-structured: pairs of heroes fight over the Evil Eye's fragments while both sides are being played. One warning about how it is printed — the four Avengers issues are collected as a block at the end rather than interleaved with Defenders #8–11, which is how Marvel lists them too, so read the two halves together rather than in the order the book prints them.
volumes.lede: Strange calls the two most antisocial people he knows and accidentally runs a team for five years.
volumes.standing: A classic, and the crossover holds up
volumes.verdict: The early Defenders is well regarded and the Avengers/Defenders War is consistently named among the best crossovers of the era — largely because it is short, structurally clean, and has an actual reason for the fight.

volumes.title: Defenders Omnibus
volumes.creators: Steve Gerber & Sal Buscema
volumes.note: Steve Gerber's run, and the strangest superhero comic Marvel published in the seventies. Gerber uses the non-team as a place to put ideas that fit nowhere else: the Headmen, four scientists who have each done something irreversible to their own skulls; Bambi and the Bozos; and the Elf With a Gun, who appears at random, murders a stranger and is never explained, because Gerber thought a universe that always explains itself is a lie. It is funny and then abruptly not. Strange spends much of it as the straight man, which is the most interesting he has ever been in a team book. The three 1950s horror shorts at the back — Mystery Tales #21, World of Fantasy #11, Tales of Suspense #9 — are reprinted as backmatter for the Headmen saga, so the volume's dates run wider than its run does.
volumes.lede: Steve Gerber's run, and the strangest superhero comic Marvel published in the seventies.
volumes.standing: A cult classic, and the most argued-about book on this shelf
volumes.verdict: Gerber's Defenders has an enormous reputation among writers — it is cited constantly as an influence by people who came up in the eighties and nineties — and it is one of the first mainstream superhero runs that is obviously authored rather than produced.

volumes.title: Doctor Strange: Master of the Mystic Arts Omnibus
volumes.creators: Steve Englehart, Frank Brunner & Gene Colan
volumes.note: The run people mean when they say Doctor Strange is the best-drawn book Marvel ever had. Frank Brunner comes off underground comix and draws Strange as Art Nouveau — whiplash linework, deep blacks, faces that actually look afraid — and Englehart writes him a story about Marvel's own universe being unmade and rebuilt by a Creator who turns out to be a frightened man. The Sise-Neg saga in Marvel Premiere #12–14 sends him back through the whole of human history to the moment of creation, and it got the Comics Code exercised for exactly the reason you would guess. Gene Colan returns for the back half and stays for years. This is also where Clea stops being a rescue object and becomes a person. Note the book stops at #22 of a run that goes to #81 — everything after 1977 is uncollected in omnibus.
volumes.lede: Four extraordinary artists in six issues, then Englehart and Brunner, then Colan for years.
volumes.standing: Widely held to be the best-drawn era the character has had
volumes.verdict: The Englehart and Brunner stretch is the one most often named when people argue for Doctor Strange as a great comic rather than a great design, and the Sise-Neg saga has a reputation well beyond the character's own readership.

volumes.title: Doctor Strange, Sorcerer Supreme Omnibus
volumes.creators: Peter B. Gillis, Roy & Dann Thomas & Jackson Guice
volumes.note: A relaunch after a year with no book at all, and it opens by taking everything off him — the Sanctum burned, his library gone, his hands broken, the title Sorcerer Supreme actually in question. Peter Gillis writes the first stretch as a rebuild from nothing, then Roy and Dann Thomas settle it into the shape it keeps for ninety issues: a working occult procedural, heavy on lore, where the magic has rules and costs and paperwork. Jackson Guice's art is the late-eighties Marvel house style at its cleanest. It is not the flashiest era on this shelf and it is the one that treats being Sorcerer Supreme as a job.
volumes.lede: A relaunch that starts by taking everything away, then settles into an occult procedural.
volumes.standing: Undervalued, and the most consistent run on the shelf
volumes.verdict: This era has a quiet, durable following. The case for it is that it is the only long stretch that takes the job seriously — the reader comes away understanding what being Sorcerer Supreme actually involves, which is not true of the flashier runs.

volumes.title: Doctor Strange, Sorcerer Supreme Omnibus
volumes.creators: Roy & Dann Thomas, Geof Isherwood & Various
volumes.note: Marvel builds a horror line around him. Rise of the Midnight Sons runs through six books at once and Strange is the one who convenes them, which makes this the second time the character's main job is assembling people who do not want to be assembled. Secret Defenders is the other half of that idea and it is a genuinely good format — a different roster every arc, picked by Strange for the specific job, none of them told why. Geof Isherwood draws most of it. It is the most nineties material on the shelf, and the Ghost Rider, Morbius and Silver Surfer chapters here are the same crossover the Ghost Rider shelf reads from the other side.
chapters: Spider-Man/Doctor Strange: The Way to Dusty Death #1
volumes.lede: Marvel builds a horror line around him, and Secret Defenders lets him assemble a new team every arc.
volumes.standing: Divisive, and Secret Defenders is better than its reputation
volumes.verdict: The Midnight Sons material is very much of its moment and readers who dislike 1990s Marvel dislike this on sight — the crossover obligations do interrupt the book repeatedly, which is the fair version of the complaint.

volumes.title: Doctor Strange, Sorcerer Supreme Omnibus
volumes.creators: David Quinn, Warren Ellis & J.M. DeMatteis
volumes.note: The end of the ninety-issue run, and it gets strange in the other sense. David Quinn writes the bulk of it, from #60 to the high seventies, and takes the book somewhere genuinely odd: Strange loses his powers and starts drawing on a substance called the Vapors, a bargain the fandom has argued about for thirty years and which is at minimum unlike anything else in the character's history. Then Warren Ellis arrives around #80 for a short, cold, very early-Ellis stretch, and J.M. DeMatteis closes the run out. Mark Buckingham draws a lot of the back half and is the best reason to look at it. The tail of the book is the odd material — an ashcan, a magazine, Kurt Busiek's 1994 Strange Tales one-shot, and What Is It That Disturbs You, Stephen?, a 1997 painted graphic novel — so the dates run past the run's own end. After this the character has no ongoing title for nineteen years.
chapters: Doctor Strange: What Is It That Disturbs You, Stephen? #1
Ghost Rider and the Midnight Sons Magazine #1
volumes.lede: The last thirty issues, in which he loses his powers and starts drawing on something called the Vapors.
volumes.standing: The low point for some readers, a cult favourite for others
volumes.verdict: The Vapors storyline is the most divisive thing on this shelf. The criticism is that it is a 1990s edginess exercise that fundamentally misreads the character — a sorcerer defined by discipline turned into an addict — and that the art through the middle stretch is inconsistent.

volumes.title: Doctor Strange by Aaron & Bachalo Omnibus
volumes.creators: Jason Aaron & Chris Bachalo
volumes.note: The first ongoing in nineteen years, and its one big idea is that magic has a price somebody has to pay. Aaron writes a Strange who eats things that are still moving, keeps a cellar full of obligations, and is quietly in enormous debt for every spell he has ever cast — which turns the character from a man with answers into a man with bills. Then the Empirikul arrive and burn magic out of the world entirely, and the back half is Strange with nothing, which is where the run gets good. Chris Bachalo draws it with the density turned all the way up: panels crammed with talking objects and impossible architecture, and a Sanctum that is clearly alive. Note the nineteen-year jump before this book — Straczynski's Strange and Vaughan and Martin's The Oath both fall in it and neither has an omnibus.
chapters: Doctor Strange: Last Days of Magic #1
volumes.lede: Magic costs something, Strange has been running a tab for years, and then someone burns magic out of the world.
volumes.standing: Well regarded, and the art is the argument
volumes.verdict: The premise is very widely praised — “magic has a cost” is the idea most often credited with making the character legible to modern readers, and it arrived alongside the film that did the same commercially.

volumes.title: Doctor Strange by Jed MacKay Omnibus
volumes.creators: Jed MacKay, Lee Garbett & Marcelo Ferreira
volumes.note: Opens by killing him, which sounds like a stunt and is actually the setup for the best thing on the modern half of this shelf. The Death of Doctor Strange is a murder mystery where the detective is a younger Strange summoned from the past to investigate his own corpse, and it is fairly played — the clues are there. Then Strange hands the book to Clea, who becomes Sorcerer Supreme of Earth and is far better at it and much less nice about it, and Jed MacKay writes ten issues of her trying to bring him back that double as the best Clea material anyone has written. The 2023 ongoing puts them both in the Sanctum as a married couple running a practice together. Lee Garbett draws the first stretch; the whole thing is unusually tightly plotted for a book about magic.
volumes.lede: A murder mystery where the detective is the victim, and then the best Clea story anyone has written.
volumes.standing: The best-reviewed modern run, and Clea is the reason
volumes.verdict: Reception has been strong and unusually consistent: the mystery is praised for actually being a mystery, and the Strange series with Clea in the lead is frequently named the best thing done with that character in her entire existence.

tone_modes.label: The best single story
tone_modes.description: The Korvac Saga. A villain who has already won, a last chapter that is an argument rather than a fight, and Pérez drawing twenty legible people in a room.

tone_modes.label: The most satisfying run
tone_modes.description: Busiek and Pérez. The Avengers as an institution with a charter and a reserve list, Ultron Unlimited, and the Kang Dynasty. If you only read one creator run, read this one.

tone_modes.label: The cosmic one
tone_modes.description: The Kree/Skrull War, and then Hickman's incursions thirty years later. Two very different ideas of what “big” means.

tone_modes.label: The bleak one
tone_modes.description: Byrne dismantling the Vision and the Scarlet Witch, and Remender's Apocalypse Twins. Neither offers you a way out.

tone_modes.label: The strangest
tone_modes.description: Englehart's Celestial Madonna. A superhero comic that becomes a cosmic religious epic and marries a woman to a plant, and means every word of it.

tone_modes.label: The one that reads like a film
tone_modes.description: The Ultimates. Hitch's six-panel widescreen pages, no continuity to know, and the direct source for most of what the films look like.

tone_modes.label: The famous disaster
tone_modes.description: The Crossing. Worth reading precisely because it is the clearest case study of 1990s plotting overriding character, and it ended the line.

tone_modes.label: The best conversation
tone_modes.description: Bendis's New Avengers. Overlapping, interrupting, unresolved talk, with the plot happening in the gaps. Nothing else here sounds like it.

tone_modes.label: The lightest
tone_modes.description: Jed MacKay's run — a team doing jobs, with an Impossible City and no thesis about what the Avengers mean. After sixty years that is a holiday.

volumes.title: Avengers Omnibus
volumes.creators: Stan Lee, Jack Kirby & Don Heck
volumes.note: The first thirty issues, and the team barely holds still for any of them. Lee and Kirby put five heroes who do not like each other in a room, lose the Hulk by issue #2, find Captain America frozen in ice in #4, and then in #16 do the thing nobody does with a hit book — they fire the entire cast and replace it with three reformed criminals and Cap. That gamble is why the Avengers is a franchise and not a Justice League tribute: the door revolves, so the roster is the story.
volumes.lede: Thirty issues in which the book invents its own premise twice and then throws the entire cast out.
volumes.verdict: Nobody disputes the importance. #4 and #16 are two of the most consequential single issues Marvel published in the 1960s, and the second one invents the format the book still runs on.

volumes.title: Avengers Omnibus
volumes.creators: Roy Thomas, Don Heck & John Buscema
volumes.note: Roy Thomas takes over and starts building the continuity engine. The Black Panther joins — the first Black superhero on an American team book — Hercules and the Black Widow drift in and out, Ultron arrives, and the Vision is built in #57 to kill the Avengers and joins them instead. John Buscema comes aboard at #41 and the book stops looking like Kirby's and starts looking like itself.
volumes.lede: Roy Thomas arrives, the Black Panther joins, Ultron is built, and in the last issue an android decides not to kill anyone.
volumes.verdict: This is where the Avengers becomes the Avengers. Three of the four most durable additions to the franchise's cast — Ultron, the Vision, the Panther on the roster — happen inside thirty issues.

volumes.title: Avengers Omnibus
volumes.creators: Roy Thomas, John Buscema & Neal Adams
volumes.note: The stretch where Thomas turns the book political and Neal Adams turns up to draw it. The Vision and the Scarlet Witch start their long unhappy romance, Yellowjacket and the Wasp marry, and #83 invents the Lady Liberators. Adams's issues on the run-up to the Kree/Skrull War are the ones people mean when they say the art changed — deep-focus figures with real weight, in a book that had been staged flat.
volumes.lede: The book turns political, Neal Adams turns up, and the romance that will define the franchise for fifty years starts.
volumes.standing: Strong, and the art changes mid-book
volumes.verdict: Well regarded, and the point where Thomas's ambitions get properly visible. The Vision/Wanda material is the single most consequential thing in it.

volumes.title: Avengers Omnibus
volumes.creators: Roy Thomas, Neal Adams & John Buscema
volumes.note: Two of the biggest things the book ever did, back to back. The Kree/Skrull War is the first Marvel story to treat the whole galaxy as the setting, and it is where Rick Jones ends a war by imagining one. Then the Avengers/Defenders War, printed here with its four Defenders chapters in reading order — the template every crossover since has copied, including the ones on this shelf that are eight books wide.
volumes.lede: The Kree/Skrull War and the Avengers/Defenders War, back to back — the book that made Marvel cosmic and the book that invented the crossover.
volumes.verdict: The Kree/Skrull War is on every shortlist of the best Avengers stories, and the Adams issues are on every shortlist of the best-drawn Marvel comics.

volumes.title: Avengers Omnibus
volumes.creators: Steve Englehart, Sal Buscema & Don Heck
volumes.note: Englehart's run, and the strangest the book has been. The Celestial Madonna saga marries Mantis to a tree, walks the Vision through his own origin as the original Human Torch, and hands Kang a defeat that takes three time periods to land. Also here: the Serpent Crown, the Squadron Supreme, Patsy Walker becoming Hellcat, and three issues of F.O.O.M. — Marvel's own fanzine — which is a genuinely odd thing to find in an omnibus and exactly right for 1975.
volumes.lede: Steve Englehart's run, the Celestial Madonna, and the most genuinely strange superhero comic Marvel was publishing.
volumes.verdict: Deeply loved by the readers who love it, and it has a strong claim to being the most imaginative run the title has had.

volumes.title: Avengers Omnibus
volumes.creators: Jim Shooter, George Pérez & John Byrne
volumes.note: Gerry Conway and then Jim Shooter, with George Pérez learning to draw crowds. The Korvac Saga is the centrepiece and it is not like the other Bronze Age epics: the villain wins, quietly, and the last chapter is the entire roster standing in a room losing an argument with a man who has already become God. Wonder Man comes back, Ultron takes another run at them, and Byrne turns up to draw the end.
volumes.lede: George Pérez arrives, and Jim Shooter writes the Korvac Saga — the story most often named the best the Avengers has.
volumes.verdict: The Korvac Saga is the story most frequently named the best Avengers story there is, and the reasons given are always the same two: the villain is sympathetic and the climax is an argument rather than a fight.

volumes.title: Avengers: West Coast Avengers Omnibus
volumes.creators: Roger Stern, Steve Englehart & Al Milgrom
volumes.note: Marvel franchises the team. Hawkeye gets a branch office in Los Angeles, four issues to prove it, and then an ongoing — and the joke that the book is the B-squad is one it makes about itself for years before Englehart quietly makes it good. Mockingbird, Wonder Man, Tigra and Iron Man in the Jim Rhodes armour; the Vision and the Scarlet Witch's own mini is printed here too, because their marriage is about to be the thing the whole line breaks over.
volumes.lede: Marvel opens a branch office. Hawkeye gets his own team, four issues to prove it works, and then an ongoing.
volumes.verdict: The received wisdom is that West Coast Avengers is the lesser book, and the received wisdom is lazy. It has a stable cast, a lead who is genuinely interesting because he is out of his depth, and it is funny on purpose.

volumes.title: Avengers: West Coast Avengers Omnibus
volumes.creators: Steve Englehart & Al Milgrom
volumes.note: Englehart's second act, and it goes places the main book never would: a time-travel arc that strands the team in the Old West and in ancient Egypt, Mockingbird letting the Phantom Rider fall, and the marriage that comes apart afterwards. This is also where the Vision is taken to pieces by a government committee and rebuilt white and blank — the single cruellest thing done to a character on this shelf, and the engine for twenty years of stories after it.
volumes.lede: Englehart's second act: time travel to the Old West and ancient Egypt, a marriage that comes apart, and the Vision taken to pieces.
volumes.verdict: Readers who value the character work rate this among the best runs of the 1980s. Readers who came for a superhero team book find it relentlessly bleak, and both are describing what is actually there.

volumes.title: Avengers by John Byrne Omnibus
volumes.creators: John Byrne, Paul Ryan & Rich Buckler
volumes.note: Byrne writing both Avengers books at once, which is why this volume is half West Coast and half the main title and reads as one thing. He picks up the white Vision and the wreckage of the Scarlet Witch's marriage and drives it all the way down — Wanda's children turn out never to have existed, and she comes apart. Then the Evolutionary War and Acts of Vengeance on top. Hard, clean, unsentimental cartooning; the plotting is another matter, and readers have argued about it for thirty-five years.
volumes.lede: Byrne writing and drawing both Avengers books at once, and finishing what West Coast started.
volumes.verdict: The craft is not in question — this is Byrne at the height of his powers as a storyteller, and the pages are a masterclass in economy.

volumes.title: Avengers: The Gathering Omnibus
volumes.creators: Bob Harras & Steve Epting
volumes.note: Bob Harras and Steve Epting's long run, which is the most underrated stretch the book has. Operation: Galactic Storm is a nineteen-part war the Avengers lose morally — they take a decision at the end that splits the team in half — and Proctor's Gatherers arc runs the Black Knight and Sersi into the ground over three years. The last issues here are the Vision and the Scarlet Witch's endgame and the start of the collapse that Onslaught finishes off.
volumes.lede: Harras and Epting's long, quiet, character-driven run — the most underrated stretch the book has.
volumes.verdict: Consistently described by the readers who know it as the most unfairly forgotten run on the title, buried between Byrne and the 1990s collapse.

volumes.title: Avengers: The Crossing Omnibus
volumes.creators: Terry Kavanagh, Bob Harras & Mike Deodato
volumes.note: The famous disaster, collected whole so you can see how it happened. Iron Man is revealed to have been Kang's agent for his entire career, a teenage Tony Stark is imported from another timeline to replace him, and the plot spills across Force Works, War Machine and Iron Man to the point that only six of these twenty-nine issues are Avengers. It is on this shelf because it is where the line ends: Onslaught follows immediately, and everything after it is a relaunch. Read it as a case study, not as a good time.
chapters: Age Of Innocence: The Rebirth Of Iron Man #1
volumes.lede: The famous catastrophe, collected whole so you can see exactly how it happened.
volumes.verdict: This is widely held to be among the worst things Marvel published in the 1990s, and unusually the criticism is specific rather than vague: the retcon is unearned, the replacement of a lead with a teenage version is transparently a marketing move, and the plot is unfollowable without four other titles.

volumes.title: Avengers by Busiek & Pérez Omnibus
volumes.creators: Kurt Busiek & George Pérez
volumes.note: Heroes Return, and the most purely satisfying run the character has. Busiek's premise is that the Avengers are an institution with thirty-five years of paperwork, and Pérez draws every page as if the roster photograph matters — which it does, because #4 is a general muster of dozens of heroes and it is legible. Avengers Forever is printed here too: twelve issues of Busiek, Roger Stern and Carlos Pacheco arguing with the whole publishing history at once, and the best time-travel comic Marvel has.
volumes.lede: Heroes Return, and the most purely satisfying run the character has — plus Avengers Forever, which argues with the whole publishing history at once.
volumes.verdict: Very widely regarded as the definitive modern Avengers run, and the one most often recommended to a reader who wants to know what the book is supposed to feel like.

volumes.title: Avengers by Busiek & Pérez Omnibus
volumes.creators: Kurt Busiek & George Pérez
volumes.note: The back half, and it goes out on Ultron. #19–22 is the story where Ultron kills the population of a country before the first page is over and the Avengers spend four issues failing to be enough — Pérez's most brutal work anywhere. Then the Kang Dynasty, the largest thing the book has attempted: Kang conquers the Earth, holds it, and the ending costs more than the win is worth. Note #55–56 and #1½ were missing from the wiki's own contents here and are restored from Marvel's collecting line.
volumes.lede: Ultron Unlimited pays off, and then the Kang Dynasty — the largest thing the book has ever attempted.
volumes.verdict: Most readers who rate the Busiek run rate this half higher: Ultron Unlimited and the Kang Dynasty are both on best-of lists in their own right.

volumes.title: Avengers by Johns & Coipel Omnibus
volumes.creators: Geoff Johns, Olivier Coipel & Ivan Reis
volumes.note: The last stretch of Avengers (1998) before Bendis takes it apart, and the volume that finally makes it available. Johns runs the team through Red Zone — a bioweapon attack on American soil, written in 2003, about exactly what you would expect — and the Search for She-Hulk, and Coipel arrives drawing figures with a weight the book had not had since Pérez. The four-issue Vision mini is here too, which is the character's own answer to what Byrne did to him.
volumes.lede: The last stretch of Avengers (1998), finally collected — and Olivier Coipel arriving.
volumes.verdict: Overshadowed on both sides — Busiek before it, Bendis after — and so it is rarely discussed at all. Readers who go back to it generally report being surprised.

volumes.title: New Avengers Omnibus
volumes.creators: Brian Michael Bendis & David Finch
volumes.note: Avengers Disassembled opens the volume — the Scarlet Witch takes the mansion apart in four issues — and then Bendis rebuilds the team out of whoever happened to be standing in a prison riot: Spider-Man, Wolverine, Luke Cage, Spider-Woman. That roster is the argument. It made the book the best-selling thing Marvel had for a decade and it made a lot of readers furious, and both reactions are about the same thing, which is that these are not the Avengers as anyone had defined them.
volumes.lede: Disassembled tears the book down, and Bendis rebuilds it with Spider-Man and Wolverine on the roster.
volumes.verdict: Commercially this is the most successful Avengers run there has been, and it set the shape of the Marvel line for a decade.

volumes.title: New Avengers Omnibus
volumes.creators: Brian Michael Bendis, Leinil Yu & Stuart Immonen
volumes.note: After Civil War the team is illegal, and the book becomes very good at being a comic about people hiding. The Illuminati mini is here — the retcon that puts Iron Man, Reed Richards and Namor in a room deciding things for everyone — and then Secret Invasion turns the paranoia literal and Dark Reign hands the country to Norman Osborn. Note the book after this one on the shelf assembles that crossover in reading order, so a couple of dozen issues appear twice, on purpose.
chapters: Breaking Into Comics the Marvel Way! #1
volumes.lede: The team is illegal, the Illuminati retcon lands, and Norman Osborn ends up running the country.
volumes.standing: The strongest half of the Bendis run
volumes.verdict: Frequently rated above the first volume by readers who like the run at all: the fugitive premise gives the cast something to do together, and the art team through this stretch is the best it had.

volumes.title: Secret Invasion by Bendis Omnibus
volumes.creators: Brian Michael Bendis, Leinil Yu & Billy Tan
volumes.note: The crossover assembled the way it was meant to be read: the eight-issue core, plus the New Avengers and Mighty Avengers issues carrying the flashbacks, printed in order rather than in blocks. The premise is the best paranoid hook Marvel has run — anyone might have been replaced, for years, and some of them were — and its problem is the one every such story has, which is that the reveal cannot be as good as the wondering. The Skrull landing in the Savage Land is where it is at its best.
volumes.lede: The crossover assembled the way it was meant to be read — the core series and the flashback issues interleaved in order.
volumes.verdict: The setup is widely admired and the Savage Land material gets consistent praise. The reading-order assembly is genuinely the best way to experience it.

volumes.title: New Avengers Omnibus
volumes.creators: Brian Michael Bendis, Stuart Immonen & John Romita Jr.
volumes.note: Ships November 2026 — it is on the shelf ahead of that because its contents, its links and its jacket are all real, which is the bar a tile has to clear. The Heroic Age relaunch: Luke Cage buys the mansion and runs an Avengers team out of it as a small business, which is the most likeable idea Bendis had on the book. Bundled with it is the first year of the flagship Avengers (2010) with John Romita Jr., which is otherwise uncollected in omnibus.
volumes.lede: The Heroic Age: Luke Cage buys the mansion and runs an Avengers team as a small business.
volumes.verdict: The Cage-led team is a favourite among readers of the Bendis run, and this stretch is generally described as the most enjoyable and least grim of it.

volumes.title: Avengers vs. X-Men Omnibus
volumes.creators: Bendis, Aaron, Brubaker, Fraction & Hickman
volumes.note: Seventy-four issues, and the honest thing to say is that most of them are X-Men comics. It is here because it is the hinge: the Phoenix Force comes back, five X-Men take it, Cyclops kills Charles Xavier, and the mutant and Avengers lines are joined at the hip for the decade after. The AVX: Vs issues are a fight comic and nothing else, which is either the best or the worst part depending on what you came for.
volumes.lede: Seventy-four issues of a line-wide war, and the hinge the whole decade turns on.
volumes.verdict: The consequences are undisputed: this is where the Avengers and mutant lines fuse, where Cyclops becomes a villain-or-not for a decade, and where Uncanny Avengers and Hickman's run both come from.

volumes.title: Avengers by Jonathan Hickman Omnibus
volumes.creators: Jonathan Hickman, Jerome Opeña & Esad Ribíc
volumes.note: Hickman runs two books as one machine. Avengers is the team getting bigger — “we have to get bigger” is the thesis and very nearly the first line — and New Avengers is the Illuminati in a dark room discovering that universes are colliding and someone has to destroy a world every few weeks. One book is about hope at scale and the other is about what the same men do when nobody is watching, and reading them interleaved, as this volume prints them, is the whole point.
chapters: Infinity: Against the Tide: Infinite Comic #1
volumes.lede: Two books run as one machine: the team getting bigger, and six men in a dark room destroying worlds.
volumes.verdict: Widely regarded as the most architecturally ambitious Avengers run ever attempted, and the New Avengers half in particular gets very high marks — the incursion premise is often called the best long-form idea Marvel has had this century.

volumes.title: Avengers by Jonathan Hickman Omnibus
volumes.creators: Jonathan Hickman, Leinil Yu & Mike Deodato
volumes.note: The second half, and it is a long controlled fall. Infinity is behind them, Time Runs Out jumps the story eight months forward with the Illuminati as fugitives and Steve Rogers hunting them, and the incursions stop being a problem to solve and become a countdown. It ends with the last two Earths in existence about to touch. Note it stops before Secret Wars itself, which is not on this shelf — that is the whole line's book, not the Avengers'.
volumes.lede: Time Runs Out: the Illuminati as fugitives, Steve Rogers hunting them, and a countdown to two Earths touching.
volumes.standing: A strong ending, with a gap in the middle
volumes.verdict: The conclusion is well regarded — the confrontation between Steve Rogers and the Illuminati is the payoff the whole structure was built for, and it delivers.

volumes.title: Uncanny Avengers Omnibus
volumes.creators: Rick Remender, John Cassaday & Daniel Acuña
volumes.note: Straight out of AvX: Captain America builds a joint Avengers/X-Men unit as a public-relations answer to a war, and Remender spends twenty-five issues showing why that does not work. The Apocalypse Twins arc goes to the end of the world and stays there — the Scarlet Witch and Rogue's argument in the middle of it is as bleak as this book gets. Cassaday opens it; Acuña's washes are what people remember.
volumes.lede: Remender's Avengers/X-Men unit, formed as public relations after a war, and taken apart over twenty-five issues.
volumes.verdict: The Apocalypse Twins arc is well regarded and Remender's willingness to let consequences stand is the most-praised thing about it.

volumes.title: Avengers: No Surrender / No Road Home Omnibus
volumes.creators: Al Ewing, Mark Waid, Jim Zub & Pepe Larraz
volumes.note: Two weekly experiments, and both are far better than a gimmick has any right to be. No Surrender is sixteen issues in sixteen weeks by three writers working as one — the Earth is stolen and the Grandmaster plays a game with it, and Ewing uses the space to give Voyager a whole invented history and then take it back. No Road Home does the same trick a year later with Nyx and a much smaller cast. Larraz and Larroca on alternating weeks and no visible seam.
volumes.lede: Two weekly experiments, written by three people at once, and far better than they have any right to be.
volumes.verdict: Reviewed far better than a weekly gimmick book was expected to be, and the Voyager conceit in particular is singled out as one of the smartest things done with an Avengers roster in years.

volumes.title: Avengers by Jason Aaron Omnibus
volumes.creators: Jason Aaron, Ed McGuinness & David Marquez
volumes.note: Ships March 2027, and it is on the shelf under the same rule as the other two unshipped books here. Aaron's premise is that the Avengers are a million years old: Celestials, an Iron Fist and a Ghost Rider in the Stone Age, and a present-day team squatting in a dead god's skull in the Arctic. It is the loudest the book has ever been and it means it — the War of the Realms and the Phoenix tournament are both in here, and McGuinness draws all of it at maximum volume.
volumes.lede: The Avengers are a million years old. Celestials, a Stone Age roster, and a team living inside a dead god.
volumes.verdict: The prehistoric Avengers conceit is the most-discussed thing in it and splits people cleanly: either a genuinely fresh mythology for a sixty-year-old property, or a gimmick stretched across four years.

volumes.title: Avengers Forever by Jason Aaron Omnibus
volumes.creators: Jason Aaron, Aaron Kuder & Jim Towe
volumes.note: The companion book, which is a Multiversal Avengers: a Ghost Rider who is Robbie Reyes, a Deathlok Wonder Man, an Ant-Man who is Tony Stark, and a Moon Knight who is Khonshu's fist, recruited against a Council of Red Skulls. It converges with the main title in Avengers Assemble, which is why this volume alternates the two and why the Alpha and Omega one-shots bracket it. Aaron's exit, and a genuinely strange, generous piece of work.
volumes.lede: A Multiversal Avengers — the wrong-universe versions of everyone — against a Council of Red Skulls.
volumes.verdict: Well liked for its invention; the alternate-universe roster is frequently called the most imaginative thing Aaron did on the franchise.

volumes.title: Avengers by Jed MacKay Omnibus
volumes.creators: Jed MacKay, C.F. Villa & Farid Karami
volumes.note: Ships May 2027. MacKay's answer to a decade of Avengers books that were about the concept of the Avengers is to write one about a team doing jobs: Captain Marvel leading, Iron Man paying for it, and a Twilight Court of villains organising against them. Blood Hunt runs through it, and so does the Impossible City, which is the best new toy the book has been given in years. This is the shelf's current end — everything after it is still coming out.
volumes.lede: After a decade of books about what the Avengers mean, one about a team doing jobs.
volumes.verdict: Reviewed well as a reset: readable, character-first, and accessible without homework, which is a specific and rare virtue on this shelf.

volumes.title: Ultimates by Millar & Hitch Omnibus
volumes.creators: Mark Millar & Bryan Hitch
volumes.note: The other Avengers, out of continuity and enormously more influential than that sounds — this is the book the films are adapted from, down to Nick Fury's face. Millar writes them as a government asset with a public-relations department and Hitch draws it “widescreen”: six panels a page, every one a shot. The second series is the better one and the harder one, because the argument it is making about American power in 2004 is not subtle and is not flattering either.
volumes.lede: Not in continuity, not the real Avengers, and by a distance the most influential Avengers comic ever published.
volumes.standing: Enormously influential, and its imitators aged badly
volumes.verdict: Routinely named one of the most important superhero comics of the century. The first series is widely regarded as excellent and the second as more ambitious and more uneven, though it was badly delayed and finished late.

tone_modes.label: Most frightening
tone_modes.description: The origin volume. McFarlane draws Venom bigger than Spider-Man, standing in his flat, talking to his wife. Nothing later on the shelf is this uncomfortable.

tone_modes.label: Most 1993
tone_modes.description: Venomnibus Vol. 1. Foil covers, a million-copy first issue, and eighteen months of three-issue miniseries about a man who lives in a sewer and eats criminals. It is not good and it is completely irreplaceable.

tone_modes.label: Best written
tone_modes.description: Agent Venom. Remender puts the symbiote on a double amputee who is also the son of an alcoholic, and never explains the metaphor once.

tone_modes.label: Best drawn
tone_modes.description: Cates and Stegman. A Venom whose silhouette changes between panels, in colour that is almost never actually black. The modern look of the character starts here.

tone_modes.label: Most horrifying
tone_modes.description: The Conway Carnage. A serial killer, a cult, an elder god and an FBI agent who cannot sleep — the only book here that reads as horror rather than as a superhero comic wearing horror.

tone_modes.label: Biggest
tone_modes.description: King in Black. Sixty-three issues, symbiote dragons over every city on Earth, and a tie-in for almost everybody Marvel publishes.

tone_modes.label: Strangest
tone_modes.description: Venomnibus Vol. 3. An eighteen-issue ongoing about a symbiote in Antarctic ice that nobody liked in 2003 and a lot of people defend now, ending with Eddie selling the suit at auction.

volumes.title: Spider-Man vs. Venom Omnibus
volumes.creators: David Michelinie, Todd McFarlane & Erik Larsen
volumes.note: The origin, and the reason this shelf does not open in 1993. Every Venom appearance from the black costume walking off Battleworld to Maximum Carnage: ASM #252 sets the suit up, #300 is where Eddie Brock puts it on and McFarlane draws the first real Venom, and the rest is Michelinie writing him as a stalker who knows where you live. The same book sits on the Spider-Man shelf, so the issue ids are shared — mark #300 read here and it is read there. Maximum Carnage is printed in crossover order, rotating Amazing, Web, Spider-Man and Spectacular month by month.
volumes.lede: The costume, the man who put it on, and every appearance up to Maximum Carnage — the only book that is on two shelves on this site.
volumes.verdict: This volume is also on the Spider-Man shelf, and that is deliberate: the issue ids are shared across the site, so Amazing Spider-Man #300 marked read here is marked read there. Both tiles carry the gold "in 2 omnibuses" pill on every issue in it.

volumes.title: Venomnibus
volumes.creators: David Michelinie, Mark Bagley & Ron Lim
volumes.note: Marvel notices Venom outsells the book he was a villain in, and hands him his own. Lethal Protector is where the turn happens — Eddie moves to San Francisco, gets a sewer full of homeless people to protect and stops being a monster on purpose. What follows is eighteen months of three-issue minis, one after another, because Marvel would not risk an ongoing: Funeral Pyre with the Punisher, The Madness with the Hulk, Nights of Vengeance, Separation Anxiety, Carnage Unleashed. Ron Lim draws most of it. It is the most 1993 object on the site and it knows it.
chapters: Silver Sable and the Wild Pack #18–19
volumes.lede: The turn from monster to anti-hero, and the beginning of the strangest publishing plan in 1990s Marvel: eighteen miniseries instead of one ongoing.
volumes.verdict: The recurring criticism is fair and is the one you should expect: the miniseries are repetitive, most run out of story by their third issue, and the volume as a whole is a monument to a sales strategy rather than to a run.

volumes.title: Venomnibus
volumes.creators: Larry Hama, Howard Mackie & Duncan Fegredo
volumes.note: The mini treadmill keeps going and starts to buckle. Sinner Takes All puts Anne Weying in the symbiote and is the best thing in the volume; The Hunger has Eddie starving for the brain chemical the suit needs; On Trial has Matt Murdock defending him in court; Tooth and Claw is Wolverine. Then Venom goes to work for the government in License to Kill and The Finale, and Marvel stops. The whole of the 1993–98 mini era ends here, and the character disappears for a year — which is the gap the next volume opens across.
volumes.lede: The treadmill runs out. Fourteen more miniseries, one genuinely good one, and the end of the character for a decade.
volumes.verdict: Readers who like the era rate this below Vol. 1 and the reason is structural rather than a matter of taste: Vol. 1 has a genuine turning point in it and this one is the same formula fourteen more times, by which point the market had noticed.

volumes.title: Venomnibus
volumes.creators: Paul Jenkins, Daniel Way & Humberto Ramos
volumes.note: Venom comes back as a Spider-Man villain again and then, in 2003, gets an ongoing at last — Daniel Way and Francisco Herrera's Venom, eighteen issues of a symbiote thawed out of Antarctic ice, which is a much stranger book than its reputation. Around it: Paul Jenkins on Peter Parker, Venom Vs. Carnage where Toxin is born, and Mark Millar's Marvel Knights arc. The volume ends with Eddie Brock dying of cancer and selling the symbiote at auction, which is the last thing that happens to this version of the character.
volumes.lede: The ongoing he was denied in 1993, ten years late — and the only Venom story that ends with a man selling his own symbiote at auction.
