volumes.verdict: The Way run was widely panned on release — the complaints were incoherence, an unlikeable cast and art that readers found hard to follow — and it has since acquired a real defence: that the incoherence is the point, that it is a horror comic rather than a superhero one, and that it is the only Venom book of its decade with an idea.

volumes.title: Agent Venomnibus
volumes.creators: Rick Remender, Cullen Bunn & Tony Moore
volumes.note: Flash Thompson lost both legs in Iraq, and the government gives him the symbiote for fifty missions with a hard time limit before it bonds permanently. Rick Remender writes it as a war comic with an addiction metaphor running underneath — the suit is the drink Flash's father could not put down — and Tony Moore draws it. Then Cullen Bunn takes it to Philadelphia, then into space, and Space Knight ends with Flash as a cosmic hero. A different man under the name, on for the reason Danny Ketch is on the Ghost Rider shelf. All 42 issues plus the point issues, complete.
volumes.lede: The symbiote as a controlled substance, worn by a double amputee with fifty missions and a hard clock. The best-written run on the shelf.
volumes.standing: Widely held to be the best-written Venom run
volumes.verdict: The Remender stretch is the one readers reach for when arguing that Venom can carry a serious book, and the addiction reading is close to consensus rather than a stretch.

volumes.title: Carnage Omnibus
volumes.creators: Zeb Wells, Clayton Crain & Gerry Conway
volumes.note: Cletus Kasady's own shelf, gathered up. It opens on Venom Vs. Carnage, which is where Toxin gets born out of Carnage the way Carnage got born out of Venom, and then runs the whole solo line: Zeb Wells and Clayton Crain's Carnage, Carnage U.S.A. where he takes a town, Superior Carnage, Deadpool vs. Carnage, and finally Gerry Conway's sixteen-issue Carnage, which turns him into an underground horror book about a cult and an elder god. A different character on a Venom shelf, on because the user put him there.
volumes.lede: Cletus Kasady's own shelf — a different character on a Venom shelf, and the volume the user put on deliberately.
volumes.verdict: The Conway/Perkins run is the volume's real recommendation and is routinely described as the best Carnage material there is and the least read. The middle stretch — Superior Carnage, AXIS, the Deadpool crossover — is where the sequel problem shows: readers generally find the character works as a threat and not as a lead.

volumes.title: Venomnibus by Cates & Stegman
volumes.creators: Donny Cates & Ryan Stegman
volumes.note: The run that reinvented the character, and the reason there is a Venom shelf to build. Cates opens by inventing Knull — a god who made the symbiotes as weapons before there was light — and rewrites everything the suit is in one issue. Ryan Stegman draws Venom as a wet, elongated, wrong-shaped thing rather than a bodybuilder, and the whole modern look of the character comes from here. Thirty-five issues plus the Web of Venom one-shots, running through Absolute Carnage and King in Black to Eddie ending up as the King in Black himself. The two events' tie-in halves are the next two tiles.
volumes.lede: The run that gave the symbiotes a god, gave Eddie a son, and reset what the character looks like. The centre of the shelf.
volumes.verdict: This is the run people mean now when they say Venom, and the consensus on it is unusually strong: the best-regarded Venom material there has been, and the one that made the character a load-bearing part of the Marvel universe rather than a Spider-Man villain with good merchandise.

volumes.title: Absolute Carnage Omnibus
volumes.creators: Donny Cates, Ryan Stegman & various
volumes.note: Cletus comes back wanting the spinal codex left behind in everyone who has ever worn a symbiote, which is a premise engineered to reach every corner of the line — and this book is that reach. The five-issue core is here (it is also in the Cates volume, so those ids are shared), and around it fourteen tie-in minis and one-shots: Deadpool, Miles Morales, Scream, Lethal Protectors, Immortal Hulk, Captain Marvel, Weapon Plus. The tail of the volume is the lead-in issues where Carnage picks his victims off one at a time.
volumes.lede: The tie-in half of the 2019 event — fourteen miniseries and one-shots around a core the previous tile already prints.
volumes.standing: Divisive — as event tie-in collections are
volumes.verdict: The core mini is generally well received: it is a deliberate Maximum Carnage homage done thirty years later with a better artist, and readers who grew up on the 1993 version rate it highly.

volumes.title: King in Black Omnibus
volumes.creators: Donny Cates, Ryan Stegman & various
volumes.note: Knull finally arrives, blacks out the sun and drops a symbiote dragon on every hero at once — the payoff Cates had been building since his first issue. Sixty-three issues: the core five, four of Venom's own, and then the widest tie-in list on this shelf, from Namor and S.W.O.R.D. to Black Cat, Savage Avengers, Thunderbolts and Return of the Valkyries. The most line-wide book here by a distance, and the reason it is on the shelf is that the Cates volume prints the core and nothing else.
chapters: King in Black: Wiccan and Hulkling #1
King in Black: Planet of the Symbiotes #1–3
King in Black: Return of the Valkyries #1–4
King in Black: Gwenom vs. Carnage #1–3
volumes.lede: Sixty-three issues — the widest book on the shelf, and the payoff of a reveal made three years earlier.
volumes.verdict: The consensus on the core is that it looks magnificent and resolves too quickly: Stegman's dragons and blacked-out cities are among the best spectacle Marvel has printed, and the ending — which turns on a very large power-up arriving late — is the most common complaint about the whole Cates era.

volumes.title: Venom War Omnibus
volumes.creators: Al Ewing, Iban Coello & various
volumes.note: Ships December 2026, and it is on the shelf ahead of that because its contents, its links and its jacket are all real, which is the bar a tile has to clear. Eddie Brock and his son Dylan both claim the symbiote and it has to choose, which is a much better hook than an event usually gets. Note where it starts: Venom (2021) #35. Al Ewing and Ram V's whole run in front of that — #1–34, the best-reviewed Venom book since Cates — has no omnibus at all, so the shelf jumps three years to get here.
volumes.lede: Ships December 2026. A father and a son with one symbiote between them — and the book that opens three years after the run in front of it stopped being collected.
volumes.standing: Not yet shipped — no verdict to report
volumes.verdict: The comics themselves ran through 2024 and were received as a solidly built event with an unusually strong central relationship and a very large number of tie-ins; the recurring criticism is the one every modern event gets, which is that the tie-in count outruns the story.

tone_modes.label: Most inventive
tone_modes.description: The Lee/Kirby imperial phase — a genuinely new idea every month, and the highest density of things-that-still-matter in Marvel's history.

tone_modes.label: Most domestic
tone_modes.description: Byrne's five years, and Waid's after them. Marriage, children, a team member quitting because he is miserable. The FF as a family that argues.

tone_modes.label: Most cosmic
tone_modes.description: Galactus and the Negative Zone in the 60s; the Council of Reeds and the multiverse in Hickman's. Both are about scale putting the family in perspective.

tone_modes.label: Most cerebral
tone_modes.description: Hickman: planned years out, structured like a novel, and fundamentally about whether Reed Richards is a good man. Demands attention and repays it.

tone_modes.label: Biggest
tone_modes.description: Millar and Hitch doing widescreen blockbuster — enormous set pieces, photo-real crowds, staged for a cinema screen.

tone_modes.label: Strangest and most charming
tone_modes.description: Fraction and Allred. Pop-art line work, a substitute team, and a book about babysitting super-genius children. Nothing else here looks like it.

tone_modes.label: Best villain
tone_modes.description: Fifteen years of Doom assembled in one place. The clearest demonstration that Marvel's best antagonist is a man with a point.

tone_modes.label: Most blue-collar
tone_modes.description: The Thing's own book — wrestling, Yancy Street, and Ben Grimm as a guy from the neighbourhood rather than a monster.

tone_modes.label: Easiest start
tone_modes.description: Ultimate FF: no continuity, young cast, modern pacing. The version to hand someone who has never read a comic.

volumes.title: Fantastic Four Omnibus
volumes.creators: Stan Lee & Jack Kirby
volumes.note: Where the Marvel Universe starts. Thirty issues and the first annual, inventing the Skrulls, Doctor Doom, the Puppet Master and Namor's return one month at a time.
volumes.lede: The first Marvel comic, and it takes a while to work out that is what it is. Watch a publisher stop making monster books and start making the modern superhero.
volumes.verdict: Read universally as essential history and uneven comics. The consensus is that the first ten or so issues are rough and fascinating, and that the book becomes genuinely great somewhere in the twenties — which is roughly when Kirby stops drawing monsters and starts designing a universe.

volumes.title: Fantastic Four Omnibus
volumes.creators: Stan Lee & Jack Kirby
volumes.note: The imperial run: the Frightful Four, the Inhumans, Wyatt Wingfoot — and #48–50, the Galactus Trilogy, which is where the book stops being a superhero comic and starts being cosmic.
volumes.lede: The best three years any superhero comic has had. Galactus, the Silver Surfer, the Inhumans, the Negative Zone, the Black Panther — all of it, in about thirty issues.
volumes.verdict: As close to a settled verdict as comics criticism produces. This stretch is routinely named the greatest sustained run in superhero comics, and #51 in particular turns up at or near the top of best-single-issue lists decade after decade.

volumes.title: Fantastic Four Omnibus
volumes.creators: Stan Lee & Jack Kirby
volumes.note: The end of Lee and Kirby together. The Black Panther's debut, Annihilus and the Negative Zone, the Kree Sentry, and Franklin Richards born.
volumes.lede: The last of Kirby, and it is still extraordinary — plus Annihilus, Franklin Richards, and a partnership visibly coming apart.
volumes.verdict: Rated just below Vol. 2 and comfortably above everything after it. The individual high points — Annual #6, the Inhumans material, the Doom stories — are as good as anything in the run.

volumes.title: Fantastic Four Omnibus
volumes.creators: Stan Lee, John Buscema & John Romita Sr.
volumes.note: After Kirby. Lee writes on with Buscema and Romita — Agatha Harkness, the Overmind, Annihilus again — and the book closes with The Lost Adventure, the Kirby story Marvel did not print until 2008. It reprints #91–93 from Vol. 3, so those three share their ids across both volumes.
volumes.lede: Life after Kirby, which turns out to be John Buscema drawing beautifully and the book quietly working out that it is now a legacy title.
volumes.verdict: Generally described as a good comic in the shadow of a great one, which is fair and slightly unkind. Buscema's art gets consistent praise and is often the reason people rate the volume at all.

volumes.title: Fantastic Four Omnibus
volumes.creators: Roy Thomas, Gerry Conway & John Buscema
volumes.note: Thomas and Conway hold the line: Thundra, Quicksilver and Crystal's wedding, and Reed shutting down his own son's mind — the decision the next twenty years keep coming back to.
volumes.lede: The 1970s properly: a rotating cast of writers, real soap-opera plotting, and a team that spends a lot of this volume broken up.
volumes.verdict: The least-discussed volume on the shelf, and the reception is mild rather than hostile: competent 1970s superhero comics with a few good stretches.

volumes.title: Fantastic Four Omnibus
volumes.creators: Roy Thomas, Len Wein, Marv Wolfman & George Pérez
volumes.note: Pérez arrives on the book that made him, and the Impossible Man, Galactus and the Brute run through it. Closes with the What If? that asks what the Marvel Bullpen would have done with the powers.
volumes.lede: The late Bronze Age, George Pérez arriving, and the issue where the Fantastic Four visit the Marvel offices and ask Stan Lee for a plot.
volumes.verdict: Sits in the shadow of the Kirby and Byrne runs and is regularly rediscovered by readers working through the shelf in order. Pérez's issues are the draw, and they hold up completely.

volumes.title: Fantastic Four by John Byrne Omnibus
volumes.creators: John Byrne
volumes.note: Writing and drawing both, Byrne makes this the best-regarded run since Kirby. Opens with the Marvel Team-Ups he drew first, then FF #232 onward — Doom, the Negative Zone, and Sue finally written as the most powerful one in the room.
volumes.lede: One person writing and drawing the book for the first time since Kirby, and the run that decided what the modern Fantastic Four is.
volumes.verdict: Universally treated as the best FF run after Lee and Kirby, and the only one usually mentioned in the same sentence. The Sue Richards material and the Doom issues are the specific things readers name.

volumes.title: Thing Omnibus
volumes.creators: John Byrne, Mike Carlin & Ron Wilson
volumes.note: Ben Grimm on his own, spun out of Byrne's run and meant to be read alongside it — which is why it sits between the two Byrne volumes here. Its first two issues are in Byrne Vol. 1 as well, and share their ids.
volumes.lede: Ben Grimm's own book, on the shelf because it is where his story actually goes when he quits the team — and because it is a different genre from everything around it.
volumes.verdict: A quiet, persistent favourite rather than a famous one. Readers who like it like it a great deal, and the reason is consistently the same: it is the only Marvel book of its era about somebody with a normal life and a bad attitude.

volumes.title: Fantastic Four by John Byrne Omnibus
volumes.creators: John Byrne
volumes.note: Secret Wars breaks the team up: the Thing stays behind on Battleworld, She-Hulk takes his chair, and Doom comes back remade. Runs to where Byrne walked off the book.
volumes.lede: The back half of the Byrne run — She-Hulk on the team, the darkest material anyone had put in this book, and an ending Byrne did not get to write.
volumes.verdict: Rated highly and less comfortably than Vol. 1. The craft is not in question; what is argued about is how dark the run gets and whether the Malice and miscarriage material is handled well — readers genuinely disagree, and the disagreement is about substance rather than taste.

volumes.title: Fantastic Four by Waid & Wieringo Omnibus
volumes.creators: Mark Waid & Mike Wieringo
volumes.note: Note the jump — Fantastic Four #296–488 has never been collected in omnibus, so sixteen years pass between this book and Byrne's last one. Waid and Wieringo restart from first principles, and Unthinkable is the best Doom story in decades.
volumes.lede: The best modern FF, and the one where the readers got a creative team un-fired.
volumes.verdict: Very widely named the best Fantastic Four since Byrne, and frequently the recommendation for a modern reader who wants to know why this team matters. Unthinkable is treated as one of the definitive Doom stories.

volumes.title: Fantastic Four by Millar & Hitch Omnibus
volumes.creators: Mark Millar & Bryan Hitch
volumes.note: Widescreen and loud: the Marquis of Death, Doom's origin retold, Ben's wedding, and Marvel 1985 collected alongside as the odd one out.
volumes.lede: Widescreen. Enormous set pieces drawn at maximum detail, and the FF treated as a blockbuster franchise rather than a family.
volumes.verdict: Splits along a clean line. Readers who want scale and momentum rate it highly; readers who come to the FF for the family find it cold and impersonal, and that is the criticism that recurs.

volumes.title: Fantastic Four by Jonathan Hickman Omnibus
volumes.creators: Jonathan Hickman, Dale Eaglesham & Steve Epting
volumes.note: The long game. The Council of Reeds, the Future Foundation, the War of Four Cities being set up years before it lands — and the death that turns Fantastic Four into FF.
volumes.lede: The most ambitious thing anyone has done with these characters: a run planned years out, about whether Reed Richards' arrogance is the problem the book has been avoiding.
volumes.verdict: Frequently named the best FF run of the 21st century and one of the best Marvel runs of its generation. The specific praise is for structure and for taking Reed seriously as a moral problem rather than a plot device.

volumes.title: Fantastic Four by Jonathan Hickman Omnibus
volumes.creators: Jonathan Hickman, Steve Epting & Barry Kitson
volumes.note: Both books at once — FF and the restored Fantastic Four, month by month — through to #611, where every thread planted in Vol. 1 is paid off at the same time.
volumes.lede: The payoff. Everything the first volume set up arrives at once, and the book becomes FF as well as Fantastic Four.
volumes.verdict: Rated alongside or slightly above Vol. 1, on the grounds that the payoff justifies the setup — which is the whole test for a run built this way.

volumes.title: Fantastic Four by Matt Fraction Omnibus
volumes.creators: Matt Fraction, Mark Bagley & Michael Allred
volumes.note: A family road trip through space and time, while a substitute team minds the Baxter Building and Allred draws them. Both Marvel NOW! series in one book.
volumes.lede: The family goes on a time-travelling holiday and a substitute team babysits. The strangest, prettiest and most divisive book on the shelf.
volumes.verdict: The two halves are received very differently, which is the key thing to know. The FF substitute-team book with Allred has a devoted following and is called one of the best things Marvel published that decade by the people who love it.

volumes.title: Fantastic Four by Dan Slott Omnibus
volumes.creators: Dan Slott, Sara Pichelli & Aaron Kuder
volumes.note: The family comes home after Secret Wars. Ben and Alicia's wedding, the Griever at the End of All Things, and Doom written as the most dangerous man alive again.
volumes.lede: The team comes back after three years off the shelf entirely, and the brief is simply: make it warm again.
volumes.verdict: Liked rather than celebrated, and that seems to be roughly what it was aiming for. The consistent praise is for getting the voices right and for treating the team as a family again after several years of not existing.

volumes.title: Fantastic Four by Dan Slott Omnibus
volumes.creators: Dan Slott, R.B. Silva & Ze Carlos
volumes.note: Ships 1 December 2026 — on the shelf ahead of that because its contents, links and jacket are all real. Slott finishes his run on the Reckoning War, the cosmic story he had been setting up since he started: the Watchers, the first war Reed ever lost, and the answer to why Uatu was watching in the first place.
chapters: Reckoning War: Trial of the Watcher #1
volumes.lede: The back half — bigger, stranger, and more willing to break things than the first.
volumes.verdict: Rated slightly above Vol. 1 by most readers, on the grounds that the run found its confidence once it no longer had to prove the family worked.

volumes.title: Doctor Doom: The Book of Doom Omnibus
volumes.creators: Stan Lee, Jack Kirby, Roy Thomas & Wally Wood
volumes.note: Latveria's side of the story, gathered across fifteen years and a dozen titles, so it doubles back over the Lee/Kirby volumes and shares their ids. Astonishing Tales and Super-Villain Team-Up are the parts hardest to find anywhere else.
volumes.lede: Fifteen years of Marvel's best villain, assembled out of everyone else's comics. Read it and the whole shelf reads differently.
volumes.verdict: Judged as a collection decision, and a good one: gathering Doom's appearances chronologically produces a genuine character study that no single run contains.

volumes.title: Ultimate Fantastic Four Omnibus
volumes.creators: Brian Michael Bendis, Mark Millar & Adam Kubert
volumes.note: A separate universe and a younger team — the accident is a teleporter, not a rocket, and Reed is a prodigy the government keeps in a building with the others. Marvel Zombies starts here.
volumes.lede: Restart them as teenagers in a government think tank. The most accessible version of the concept anyone has made, and the accidental birthplace of Marvel Zombies.
volumes.verdict: Regarded as one of the better Ultimate books without being one of the great ones. The consistent recommendation is as an entry point: it is genuinely the easiest book on this shelf to hand to a new reader.

volumes.title: Ultimate Fantastic Four Omnibus
volumes.creators: Mike Carey, Mark Millar & Pasqual Ferry
volumes.note: Ultimate Doom, the back half of Ultimate Extinction, and the crossovers that close the line out before Ultimatum ends it.
volumes.lede: The back half of the Ultimate run, where it stops being an introduction and starts damaging its own cast.
volumes.verdict: Reception is softer than Vol. 1's. The writing is generally considered stronger and the tone considerably less fun, and readers who came for the accessible version report the second volume being a different book.

tone_modes.label: Most character-driven
tone_modes.description: The fallout volume — a team scattered, Xavier rebuilding himself, and the quiet work of deciding what the X-Men are for now.

tone_modes.label: Darkest
tone_modes.description: X-Force and the Messiah War. A black-ops mutant kill squad and a post-apocalyptic future. This is the era at its most brutal.

tone_modes.label: Most political
tone_modes.description: Utopia — Norman Osborn running national security, and the X-Men responding by seceding onto an island. The direct ancestor of Krakoa.

tone_modes.label: Biggest
tone_modes.description: Necrosha and Second Coming. The whole line pointed at one story, and a finale that actually costs something.

volumes.title: X-Men: Divided We Stand Omnibus
volumes.creators: Carey, David, Kyle & Yost, Brubaker
volumes.note: What Messiah Complex left on the floor. The mansion is rubble, the team is formally disbanded, Xavier's body is missing and Cable has jumped into the future with the first mutant born in a decade. Four books pick the pieces up at once — Carey rebuilding Xavier inside his own fractured head, Peter David watching Mutant Town drain out, Kyle & Yost standing up the black-ops X-Force that Cyclops will not admit exists, and Brubaker walking everyone west. Closes with the X-Men housed in San Francisco, which is the status quo for the next three books.
volumes.lede: The fallout. A team that has broken up, a leader shot in the head, and the line quietly deciding what the X-Men are for now.
volumes.verdict: Carey's X-Men Legacy is the sleeper of the whole era and is regularly named by readers as the best-written X-book of its period — a slow, careful character study running underneath a line full of events.

volumes.title: X-Men: Messiah War Omnibus
volumes.creators: Swierczynski, Kyle & Yost, Fraction
volumes.note: The middle chapter of the trilogy, with the year that walks into it. Cable is still running through time with Hope; Cyclops sends X-Force after him, and the two books trade chapters across eighty years of ruin with Stryfe and Apocalypse waiting at the end of it. Around that core: the Sisterhood, Lovelorn, X-Factor's Secret Invasion detour, and Old Ghosts — which is where Selene first starts pulling the thread that becomes Necrosha. Nobody comes back from the future the same.
volumes.lede: The middle chapter of the trilogy, and the darkest stretch on this shelf: a child raised on the run through a ruined future, with a kill squad sent after her.
volumes.verdict: Swierczynski's Cable is widely underrated and is the part of this era readers most often say they were surprised by — a genuinely affecting book about a soldier and a baby, in a line otherwise doing events.

volumes.title: X-Men: Utopia Omnibus
volumes.creators: Fraction, Carey & Peter David
volumes.note: Norman Osborn's Dark Reign reaches San Francisco, and the X-Men answer it by raising Asteroid M out of the bay and declaring it a country. Utopia is the crossover; Nation X is life on the island afterwards — Magneto walks in, Namor brings Atlantis, and the cast that matters in Second Coming is assembled here. Rogue's Salvage arc opens the book and X-Factor renumbers to #200 alongside it. Two of the eight Utopia chapters are Dark Avengers issues, printed here because the crossover does not parse without them.
volumes.lede: Norman Osborn is running national security, and the X-Men respond by seceding from the United States onto an island. The most political volume on the shelf.
volumes.verdict: Reception at the time was mixed — the Dark Reign crossover elements were criticised as an interruption, and Osborn-as-everything was wearing thin line-wide by 2009.

volumes.title: X-Men: Second Coming Omnibus
volumes.creators: Kyle & Yost, Carey, Fraction & Swierczynski
volumes.note: Necrosha first — Selene raising every dead mutant on Genosha while X-Force is still holding a line nobody knows about — then Cable and Hope finally walking home, and then fourteen chapters of the finale. Bastion's Nimrods, the dome over San Francisco, and the deaths the saga has been driving at since Messiah Complex. X-Force #28 is both a chapter of the event and the last issue of that series, which is the neatest thing this book does.
volumes.lede: The finale. Necrosha first, then Hope comes home, and the trilogy pays what it owes.
volumes.verdict: Second Coming is very well regarded and is generally treated as one of the better X-Men crossovers — specifically because it was allowed to have consequences that stuck, which the line had been bad at for years.
